detail.title: Field of Education and Political Behavior: Predicting GAL/TAN Voting

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.ethicsApproval: The authors affirm this research did not involve human participants.
declarations.funderStatement: This research was funded by the Advanced European Research Council grant TRANSNATIONAL (#885026) administered by the Robert Schuman Centre, EUI, Florence, and the Kenan and Burton Craige Research Foundations at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill.

publicationDetails.detailsText: American Political Science Review, volume 119, issue 2, 2025[10.1017/S0003055424000583]

detail.abstract: Education is perhaps the most generally used independent variable in the fields of public opinion and vote choice. Yet the extent to which a person is educated is just one way in which education may affect political beliefs and behavior. In this article, we suggest that the substantive field of education has an independent and important role to play over and above level. Using cross-national evidence for 15 European countries we find that a person's field of education is robustly significant and substantively strong in predicting voting for GAL and TAN parties that have transformed European party systems. Analysis of panel data suggests that the effect of educational field results from self-selection, a direct effect during education, and a post-education effect in occupation.

title: The Structural Selection of Nominal Human-in-the-Loop: Technical and Market Erosion Pressures in Accountability-Deficient AI Governance

detail.title: The Structural Selection of Nominal Human-in-the-Loop: Technical and Market Erosion Pressures in Accountability-Deficient AI Governance
detail.abstract: In 2025, a private student loan company in the United States reached an administrative settlement after its AI-driven lending assessments were found to have produced discriminatory effects. Accountability procedures were activated, yet legal liability was never established, and the verification of remedial measures was left to the regulated entity itself. This paper focuses on that structure. In domains where AI has become the de facto decision-maker, human involvement is formally maintained whilst the institutional means for externally verifying its substance remain absent. This paper defines that condition as 'nominal human-in-the-loop' (nominal HITL) and presents a diagnostic framework comprising three Accountability Regime (AR) indicators for identifying the institutional conditions under which it arises. It further identifies two generative mechanisms: technical opacity and market competitive pressure. The assessment of institutional conditions is operationalised through an Independent Evaluating Instance (IEI) specification that relies not on the self-reporting of the observed entity but on observation of publicly available primary documents. The contribution of this paper lies in formulating the institutional conditions under which the substance of human oversight is undermined in a manner that can be confirmed through independent documentary observation.

title:
Housing Dereliction in a Superstar City: 
Future Gains, Today's Neglect, and Disamenity Effects
affiliations: and Seijo University

detail.title:
Housing Dereliction in a Superstar City: 
Future Gains, Today's Neglect, and Disamenity Effects
detail.abstract: Why do derelict houses persist in urban areas despite strong demand, and what are their effects on neighbourhoods? This paper sheds light on a simple mechanismspeculation over future real estate value increasesthat explains this puzzle, and employs empirical strategies to test this mechanism and quantify the disamenity effects of derelict houses. First, we develop a dynamic discrete choice model showing that expectations of future urban regeneration can incentivise property owners to delay redevelopment, thereby prolonging dereliction. Using variation induced by urban regeneration plans in central Tokyo, we find that properties located in designated regeneration areas are 6-14% more likely to be derelict. Second, we estimate the effect of derelict houses on nearby rents using future regeneration plans as an instrumentaffecting dereliction but not current rents directly. Our 2SLS results show that one additional derelict house within 80 metres reduces rents by 1.5% on average. The effect is magnified to up to 4.5% in areas with low accessibility to public safety services, suggesting that renters' concerns about fire and crime risks amplify the disamenity effects of derelict properties. Our findings suggest that rational forward-looking behaviour can reduce effective housing supply and generate negative neighbourhood externalities, highlighting an unintended consequence of place-based urban regeneration policies.

title: Preventing Transfer Pricing Disputes Under Brazil's New Regime: Structural Limits of the Unilateral APA Under Law No. 14,596/2023 and the Constitutional Challenge of Regulatory Design
affiliations: University of Coimbra Institute for Legal Research

detail.title: Preventing Transfer Pricing Disputes Under Brazil's New Regime: Structural Limits of the Unilateral APA Under Law No. 14,596/2023 and the Constitutional Challenge of Regulatory Design
detail.abstract: This article critically examines the Brazilian regime for preventing transfer pricing disputes under Law No. 14,596/2023. It argues that, although substantive convergence with the arm's length standard represents significant progress, the regulation of Article 38, pending since the August 2024 public consultation, presents structural weaknesses that tend to compromise the instrument's preventive function: the exclusively unilateral configuration, the linkage to the CONFIA programme as an admissibility filter, administrative discretion to limit applications, the inadequacy of Brazil's tax treaty network, and the lack of provisions on the relationship between the APA and the federal tax administrative procedure (DRJs and CARF). Through normative, doctrinal, and comparative analysis, the article identifies tensions with the constitutional principles of tax legality, equality, and due process, and formulates six concrete normative proposals for regulatory improvement.

title: Market Disappointment with Central Bank Announcements
affiliations: and University of Orleans - Laboratoire d'économie d'Orléans

detail.title: Market Disappointment with Central Bank Announcements
detail.abstract: We introduce an index of market disappointment caused by the content of each central bank announcement for both the Fed and the ECB. To detect this disappointment, we analyze articles from leading financial newspapers and identify sentences that convey it. The index enables us to uncover new facts about the market response to central bank announcements. First, we document that disappointment with central bank announcements is frequently reported (in about 20% of the announcements) and predominantly stems from the absence of easing measures. Second, we find that market disappointment is associated with immediate revisions in the perceived monetary policy rule, which contrasts with previous findings based on standard surprise measures. Third, we show that disappointment leads to declines in stock prices and increases in volatility over the subsequent days. These effects are economically significant and present for the announcements of both the Fed and the ECB, controlling for standard monetary policy surprise measures. The reversal pattern and results from additional analysis are consistent with an investor-sentiment-based explanation for these effects.

title: Tax Salience under Rational Inattention
affiliations: Yokohama City University, Yokohama City University - Graduate School of International Management, Yokohama City University and Yokohama City University

detail.title: Tax Salience under Rational Inattention
detail.abstract: This paper examines how tax salience and limited attention shape consumer demand and store choice. Using nationwide survey data on retailers' price display formats, point-of-sale (POS) data, and consumer expenditure panels, we document three main findings. First, demand is approximately 3% higher in stores using tax-exclusive price displays than in those using tax-inclusive displays, indicating systematic underreaction to less salient taxes. This pattern is short-lived and tends to dissipate within about three months, consistent with gradual learning. Second, we show that responses operate along both the intensive and extensive margins, particularly among high school graduates. In addition to increasing purchase quantities, these consumers shift their shopping toward tax-exclusive stores. Importantly, this store-switching behavior arises even when underlying prices are identical across stores, indicating that salience alone affects the allocation of demand across sellers. Third, we document substantial heterogeneity in responses, with less-educated consumers exhibiting stronger demand responses and more frequent store switching, consistent with differences in information-processing costs. We develop a simple rational-inattention framework that unifies these findings, showing how heterogeneous attention costs generate underreaction, store-switching behavior, and transitory patterns as consumers learn over time.

title: Coding Open-ended Responses with Large Language Models: Evidence from Three Economic Experiments
affiliations: Pontificia Universidad Javeriana and Pontificia Universidad Javeriana

detail.title: Coding Open-ended Responses with Large Language Models: Evidence from Three Economic Experiments
detail.abstract: This paper examines whether large language models (LLMs) can reliably code openended responses and free-form communication data in experimental economics. We apply three LLMs (GPT, Claude, and Gemini) under alternative prompt designs and temperature settings to data from three published experiments that differ in coding structure, the degree of textual ambiguity, and the role of communication in the experimental design. In a trust game where the coding task targets explicit commitment language, all three models achieve strong agreement with human benchmarks (Cohen's κ > 0.80) and replicate the finding that promise-making predicts cooperative behavior. In thematic coding of explanations for discrepancies between self-and peer-reported AI use, LLMs reliably recover the dominant category but over-identify rare inductively derived categories by a factor of three to five. In multi-label coding of chat communication in a coordination experiment, agreement is weaker and downstream regressions do not replicate consistently, with some coefficients reversing sign. Model choice and temperature are not first-order determinants of performance. The primary constraint is the structural fit between the coding scheme and LLM capabilities: LLMs succeed when categories are deductively defined and explicitly marked in the text, and fail when coding relies on pragmatic inference or inductively derived themes. These findings have direct implications for measurement reliability and analytical transparency in experimental research that uses coded text.

title: College Sports Reform and the Sports Broadcasting Act of 1961
affiliations: Indiana University - Kelley School of Business - Department of Business Law

detail.title: College Sports Reform and the Sports Broadcasting Act of 1961
detail.abstract:
Recent proposals to reform college sports have seized on an unlikely statutory vehicle: the Sports Broadcasting Act of 1961 ("SBA"). Originally enacted to allow certain U.S. professional sports leagues to pool their television broadcast rights, the SBA has emerged as a potential solution to intercollegiate athletics' mounting financial instability, as the vast majority of athletic departments spend millions of dollars more each year than they generate. Advocates contend that extending the statute to college sports would allow the industry to aggregate its media rights, negotiate more lucrative broadcast agreements, and use the resulting revenue to preserve the existing college sports model, including women's and Olympic sports. 

This Article argues that these proposals are unlikely to achieve their stated goals. A narrow amendment modeled on the existing SBA would be of limited value because the statute protects only "sponsored telecasting," leaving agreements with cable and streaming providers outside its scope. A broader amendment covering all media rights would be more consequential but also more troubling. Although such an exemption might increase industry revenue, it would not address the spending incentives that have long driven athletic departments into persistent budgetary strain. Instead, new revenue would likely be absorbed into the same competitive arms race that produced the current crisis. 

Nor would expanded antitrust immunity come without cost. The same consolidation that would allow college sports to extract higher media-rights fees would likely reduce competition, restrict output, and increase prices, shifting additional costs onto viewers. The Article therefore contends that SBA reform misdiagnoses a predominantly spending-driven crisis as a mere revenue shortfall. Rather than stabilizing intercollegiate athletics, extending the SBA to college sports would risk preserving an already unstable model while imposing greater costs on the viewing public.

title: The Third Triumvirate: Three Flow Empires and the Solar Threshold What the Beijing Summit Documents Beneath the Marketing Surface of Trade Negotiation
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: The Third Triumvirate: Three Flow Empires and the Solar Threshold What the Beijing Summit Documents Beneath the Marketing Surface of Trade Negotiation

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests. This work was conducted as independent research without institutional affiliation, sponsorship, or external commission.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This paper is a theoretical and analytical work based on publicly available sources. It involves no human subjects, no patient data, and no participant interactions.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. The work was conducted by the author as independent geostrategic research.

detail.abstract: The Trump-Xi summit that opened in Beijing on May 14, 2026, has been received in international coverage through two principal narratives: a historic deal reshaping the relationship between two empires, or a confrontational turn exposing the depth of the rivalry. Both framings rest on the same assumption-that the summit is an open event whose outcome will be determined by the dynamics of the negotiation itself. This paper offers a different reading. The summit is not an open event; it is a documentary act. And it does not stand alone-it is one moment in a wider structural transformation that the classical vocabulary of international relations does not yet name. The argument is that what is being documented in Beijing is the formation of a Third Triumvirate-the direct coordination of the three founding flow constitutions of the Global Flow System (the American liquidity order, the Chinese production-logistics order, the Russian physical-substrate order), bypassing the classical polis-state mediation layers. The parallel with the classical Roman triumvirates of 60 BCE and 43 BCE is not rhetorical decoration. Both the structural kinship and the structural difference reveal what is now happening. The paper sets out the formation of the Third Triumvirate from its first publicly documentable move in July 2024 through the four dated crystallization events of 2025-2026, distinguishes it from the classical pattern on two structural axes (absence of the hidden weaker-third asymmetry; absence of the institutional counterweights of collegialitas and annuitas), reads the summit's American system-delegation as direct flow-constitution coordination rather than diplomatic encounter, and locates the Solar System as the new extensive space toward which the strategic tension of a closed terrestrial system is now turning. The paper closes with two scenarios-structural consolidation or breakdown into internal conflict-and reads Xi's opening reference to Thucydides, rather than Sun Tzu, as the first visible brick in the construction of a shared frame that the three flow constitutions, unlike the classical Roman triumvirs, do not inherit.

title: Not Yet: Humans Outperform LLMs in a Colonel Blotto Tournament
affiliations: New Economic School (NES), , National Research University Higher School of Economics, Central Economics and Mathematics Institute, Russian Academy of Sciences (CEMI RAS) and National Research University – Higher School of Economics (HSE University)

detail.title: Not Yet: Humans Outperform LLMs in a Colonel Blotto Tournament

declarations.funderStatement: The study was supported by a grant from the Russian Science Foundation, No. 25-18-00539, https://rscf.ru/project/25-18-00539/.

detail.abstract: The emergence of large language models (LLMs) has spurred economists to study how humans and LLMs behave in strategic settings. We organized a series of round-robin tournaments in the Colonel Blotto game. This game attracts game theorists' attention due to high-dimensional action space and the absence of pure strategy Nash equilibria. In the first tournament, more than 200 human participants competed against one another. In the second tournament, several popular LLMs were invited to submit strategies. In the third tournament, we matched the number of LLM strategies to the number submitted by humans. We find that humans more often employ better-calibrated intermediate-level allocation heuristics and outperform the simpler, more stereotyped strategies submitted by LLMs. Strategic sophistication is key to success if and only if the necessary level of reasoning depth is reached, while lower and higher levels of reasoning offer no clear advantage over the primitive strategies. Among humans, field of study weakly predicts success: participants with STEM backgrounds perform better in the first tournament. Surprisingly, humans almost do not adjust their strategies across tournaments with different sets of opponents. This result suggests that humans base their choices primarily on the game's rules rather than on the identity of their opponents, treating LLMs much like human competitors.

title: Man v Machine: A 24/7 Human-AI Market Simulation for Behavioural FinTech Research
affiliations: University of York

detail.title: Man v Machine: A 24/7 Human-AI Market Simulation for Behavioural FinTech Research
detail.abstract: The stock market is chaos-a complex adaptive system that has defied complete understanding for decades. Experimental finance has historically relied on isolated lab sessions and brief human participation. Man v Machine removes these constraints. It is a persistent, 24/7 trading simulation where humans and configurable AI agents compete continuously on a shared leaderboard. The market never stops. Data accumulates at scale. Real-time herding metrics (Cross-Sectional Standard Deviation of returns, CSSD; Christie & Huang, 1995) are calculated each cycle, with every trade and portfolio snapshot logged to a permanent archive. The platform is a research instrument, a competitive trading game, and a living market-all in one. Unlike many closed simulation frameworks that exist, Man v Machine is a live, operational platform, generating continuous empirical behavioural data. The simulation is free and open to everyone. Researchers can purchase access to a private game mode, creating a configurable virtual laboratory with full data export. A sample research report from a 10-minute session is available on Zenodo (Magar, 2026).

reference: Journal of Geoeconomics, volume 1, 2026[10.65963/jgeoecon.2026.83714]
title: China’s Anti-Dumping Investigation on Pork Imports from Europe: A Calibrated Retaliation
affiliations: Bruegel and Bruegel

detail.title: China’s Anti-Dumping Investigation on Pork Imports from Europe: A Calibrated Retaliation
detail.abstract: This case study explores China’s ongoing retaliation against the EU through an anti-dumping investigation of EU pork, after the EU conducted an antisubsidy investigation into Chinese-produced electric vehicles (EVs). China’s pork probe aimed to sway key EU Council votes on EV tariffs, targeting Spain as the largest pork exporter—especially of offal, which is difficult to export elsewhere. Furthermore, China considered Spain particularly vulnerable to its influence because of its ambition to receive investment from China into green technology sectors, including EV and battery factories. We find this case instructive, as a continuation of China’s policy to pit the economic interests of EU Member States against one another, with negative consequences for the EU’s overall leverage. A policy recommendation to be drawn from this case study is for the EU to build internal protection against Member States playing against EUlevel interests in trade and investment.

title: Heterogeneous Equity Responses to Forward Guidance Shocks: An Asset Pricing Perspective
affiliations: University of Göttingen, University of Göttingen and University of Göttingen

detail.title: Heterogeneous Equity Responses to Forward Guidance Shocks: An Asset Pricing Perspective
detail.abstract: We examine the heterogeneous effects of Federal Reserve forward guidance on equity returns. Using structural high-frequency shocks identified by Jarociński (2024), we distinguish between Delphic and Odyssean forward guidance and estimate their dynamic effects on equity returns. Consistent with flight-to-safety mechanisms, we find that Delphic forward guidance shocks generate significant response heterogeneity across Fama-French portfolios. For instance, during 'risk-off' episodes, profitability is favored over firm size. By contrast, Odyssean forward guidance produces largely symmetric responses across all portfolios. We link the muted heterogeneity of responses to Odyssean shocks to highly informed and efficient markets. Our results have important implications for portfolio managers aiming to hedge against policy-induced uncertainty, and for policymakers designing communication strategies that acknowledge the heterogeneous transmission of forward guidance across firms.

title: Believing and Practicing: How Religion Shapes Human Capital and Growth
affiliations: Monash University - Department of Economics, University of Tokyo and Monash University - Department of Economics

detail.title: Believing and Practicing: How Religion Shapes Human Capital and Growth
detail.abstract: We develop a dynamic model in which individuals allocate time between work and religious activities, and parents invest in their children's human capital and religious belief. The model delivers, in a unified framework, the two empirical regularities documented by Barro and McCleary (2003) and McCleary and Barro (2019): controlling for religious activities, stronger belief raises economic growth because it raises human capital investment; controlling for belief, more time spent on religious activities lowers growth by crowding out labor supply. While the labor-supply margin is individually optimal, the human-capital margin is not: parents do not internalize that greater human-capital investment crowds out future religious transmission through the socialization channel, leading to inefficiently high human capital in equilibrium under strong socialization externality. We extend this baseline framework in three directions. First, introducing a complementarity between religious belief and human capital-capturing the Protestant-ethic channel of Weber (1930)-we show that the efficiency of equilibrium depends non-monotonically on the strength of this complementarity. Second, allowing for cultural conflict between two religious groups à la Bisin and Verdier (2000), we show that cultural intolerance depresses human capital investment and, if human capital raises labor productivity, reduces economic growth. Third, embedding the model in a system of cities, we show that larger, more productive cities endogenously attract workers who invest more in human capital and spend less time on religious activities, generating a negative cross-city relationship between city size and religiosity that is consistent with the empirical evidence in McCleary and Barro (2019).

title: Social Media Censorship, Policy Targeting and Electoral Competition
affiliations: London School of Economics & Political Science (LSE)

detail.title: Social Media Censorship, Policy Targeting and Electoral Competition
detail.abstract: We study electoral competition when the incumbent party controls a social media platform and strategically censors public opinion. Within-country panel evidence from electoral autocracies shows that higher censorship is associated with more targeted policy in political competition, the opposite of what a simple substitution story would predict. To explain this pattern, we extend the probabilistic voting framework of Lindbeck and Weibull (1987) to incorporate strategic censorship operating through the visible distribution of public sentiment. A uniform censorship rule partitions the electorate into two sets: groups with concentrated valence opinions remain policy-contested, while groups with dispersed opinions are censorship-captured and dropped from the policy calculus entirely. The model further predicts that this distortion is increasing in platform credibility, a prediction we validate using crosscountry data on social media trust from the Reuters Institute Digital News Report.

title: The Tariff-Autonomy Paradox: Climate-Smart Goods and the UK Global Tariff

detail.title: The Tariff-Autonomy Paradox: Climate-Smart Goods and the UK Global Tariff
detail.abstract: Can tariff autonomy deliver green trade liberalization when statutory tariff cuts are not the binding barrier? This paper studies the United Kingdom Global Tariff (UKGT), the United Kingdom's post Brexit most favored nation (MFN) tariff schedule, and asks whether tariff cuts on climate-smart goods increased realized imports. The analysis compares UK imports with imports by 27 European Union (EU) member states over 2017 to 2023 for non-EU partners and an externally defined universe of 64 HS6 climate smart goods. The preferred PPMLHDFE specification absorbs reporter partner product, reporter partner year, and product year fixed effects, allowing the comparison to be made within stable sourcing relationships while controlling for bilateral annual shocks and global product year shocks. The results reveal a tariff autonomy paradox. Larger UKGT tariff cuts are associated with weaker, not stronger, UK import performance. A one percentage point larger tariff cut is associated with about 11.2% lower import value relative to EU reporters, with the effect concentrated among MFN relevant partners and weak among preferential partners. Mechanism tests show lower imports, fewer suppliers, and higher sourcing concentration. The policy implication is that green trade liberalization is not equivalent to effective liberalization unless tariff reform is paired with measures that reduce nontariff frictions and broaden sourcing networks.

title: Designing Donor Registries: Behavioral Drivers of Enrollment and Giving
affiliations: University of Economics in Bratislava,  and University of Technology Sydney (UTS)

detail.title: Designing Donor Registries: Behavioral Drivers of Enrollment and Giving
detail.abstract: Many charitable organizations invite potential donors to first join a registry before soliciting donations from those who have joined. Behavioral theories suggest that the choice architecture of registry enrollment can influence not just participation but also future giving. Some approaches may be relatively more likely to increase the likelihood of joining but reduce the subsequent propensity to donate and the amount donated, while other methods might have the opposite effect. We experimentally test four behavioral theories-overhead aversion, status quo bias, reciprocity, and moral consistency-in a two-stage donor engagement model. We find that (1) disclosing registry-related overhead costs decreases donations, (2) changing the default enrollment method (op-in vs. opt-out) does not affect enrollment nor donations, (3) targeting reciprocity by offering a small gift conditional on joining the registry boosts enrollment but not donations, and (4) targeting moral consistency by requesting an upfront contribution does not decrease the likelihood of joining the registry and can improve charity returns. Our findings emphasize how subtle differences in the design of early-stage donor approaches can influence longer-term fundraising outcomes.

title: Proof-of-Conviction: A Cryptoeconomic Framework for Type-Sorting Token Distribution through Enforced Illiquidity and Continuous-Time Screening

detail.title: Proof-of-Conviction: A Cryptoeconomic Framework for Type-Sorting Token Distribution through Enforced Illiquidity and Continuous-Time Screening

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is the founder and sole developer of Streamlock, the protocol whose mechanism is formalized in this paper. The paper describes and analyzes a mechanism designed and implemented by the author.

detail.abstract: Token distribution mechanisms in cryptocurrency markets overwhelmingly rely on immediate resale liquidity (λ = 1), creating an adverse selection environment in which no observable behavior distinguishes high-conviction participants from short-horizon extractors. This paper introduces a novel primitive: exit timing as a priced signal of conviction. By formalizing the liquidity spectrum λ — the fraction of purchased tokens on which the protocol imposes a binding resale restriction at the point of purchase — we show that at λ = 1, token markets exhibit coordination failures consistent with the noise-trader model (De Long et al., 1990) and adverse selection dynamics (Akerlof, 1970), producing a race-to-liquidity in which early exit is individually rational regardless of conviction. Empirical evidence supports these predictions: fewer than 1.4% of tokens on pump.fun graduate to sustained trading, 84.7% of major 2025 token launches trade below their offering price, and buyback programs totaling over $70 million have failed to durably support prices at revenue-generating protocols. We formalize Proof-of-Conviction, a mechanism in which λ = 0 at purchase for all participants and exit is gated by a milestone-dependent state machine (GRIND → FREEZE → UNLOCK) with a linear fee decay from 50% to 1% during unlock windows. The fee schedule transforms exit timing into a priced signal: when a holder exits and how much they pay reveals information about their private valuation. We prove two results that formalize this: non-exiters reveal a lower bound on their reservation value (Theorem 4.1), and exiters reveal a bracketed type interval through their choice of exit time (Corollary 4.2). Together, these results constitute a screening mechanism in the Rothschild-Stiglitz (1976) tradition that produces monotone sorting of holder types through observable behavior. The purchase decision becomes a costly commitment, and exit timing becomes a type-revealing signal. Proof-of-Conviction is presented as a conviction-revealing primitive that any mechanism designer can adopt, not as a complete token distribution system.

title: Reliability Inference for Multicomponent Stress-Strength Model Based on the Half-Logistic Geometric Distribution Under Progressive Type-II Censoring
affiliations: Misr Higher Institute for commerce and computers, Tanta University, Suez Canal University, Suez Canal University, Tanta University, Tanta University and Suez Canal University

detail.title: Reliability Inference for Multicomponent Stress-Strength Model Based on the Half-Logistic Geometric Distribution Under Progressive Type-II Censoring
detail.abstract: The assessment of multicomponent system reliability is an essential issue in reliability engineering, particularly when component lifetimes are only partially observed due to censoring. This study investigates the estimation of the multicomponent stress--strength reliability parameter for an \(s\)-out-of-\(k\) system when both stress and strength variables follow the half-logistic geometric (HLG) distribution under progressive Type-II censoring. An explicit expression for the reliability measure is obtained, representing the probability that at least \(s\) of the \(k\) strength components successfully withstand the applied stress. Statistical inference is developed from both frequentist and Bayesian methods. Maximum likelihood estimation is employed for point estimation, while interval estimation is carried out using asymptotic and bootstrap-based procedures. For Bayesian inference, different loss functions are considered using both Lindley’s approximation and Markov chain Monte Carlo technique. The corresponding Bayesian interval estimates are obtained through credible and highest posterior density intervals. The performance of the inference techniques are examined through an extensive Monte Carlo study conducted under multiple progressive censoring schemes and prior specifications. A real data application is included to demonstrate the practical usefulness of the proposed methodology.

title: Rent Control: Does it work?

detail.title: Rent Control: Does it work?
detail.abstract: Rent controls have well-intentioned goals, including reducing rental burdens and ensuring access to affordable housing. But these regulations can generate unintended consequences, stifling housing supply, reducing labour mobility, and driving up rents in unregulated dwellings.

detail.abstract: The financial sustainability of the U.S. healthcare system is continuously challenged by potential billing irregularities and resource allocation inefficiencies. Traditional audit mechanisms often rely on manual heuristics, which struggle to scale across massive datasets. In this paper, we propose an unsupervised machine learning framework to identify and prioritize flagged pricing anomalies within public Medicare claims data. Using PySpark for large-scale data processing, we applied an Isolation Forest algorithm to a 5% analytical sample of provider-service billing records (N = 482,771), evaluating the expected relationship between service volume and billing markup. In accordance with a predefined contamination threshold of 0.01, the model isolated approximately 1% of records as extreme pricing anomalies, representing an estimated upper-bound financial exposure of up to USD 20.8 billion before audit validation. Additional geographic and specialty-level normalization showed that flagged exposure was highly concentrated, with Osteopathic Manipulative Medicine and states such as Washington, Alaska, and California exhibiting the highest average flagged exposure per providerservice billing record. These findings suggest that targeted, AI-assisted audit strategies can help identify concentrated exposure patterns at scale, thereby supporting more efficient allocation of government audit resources and improving fiscal oversight of public healthcare expenditures.

title: Neuromechanical Coupling Between Ground Reaction Torque and Distal Kinematics in Ballistic Strikes: A Granger Causality Approach
affiliations: Universidade do Porto, Universidade do Porto and Universidade do Porto

detail.title: Neuromechanical Coupling Between Ground Reaction Torque and Distal Kinematics in Ballistic Strikes: A Granger Causality Approach
detail.abstract: Ballistic strikes require integrating propulsive forces with distal stabilization, yet traditional zero-dimensional analyses assume simplified, unidirectional energy transfer. This study investigated directional neuromechanical coupling between distal kinematics (velocity, [[EQUATION]]) and support kinetics (net vertical ground reaction torque, [[EQUATION]]). Karate athletes ([[EQUATION]]) performed maximal-velocity strikes across anterior-oriented (AOS), symmetrical lateral (SLS), and posterior-weighted stances (PWS) to manipulate inter-limb load distributions. Continuous trajectories were evaluated via one-dimensional Statistical Parametric Mapping (SPM1D, [[EQUATION]]). Dynamic directional coupling was quantified using sliding-window Granger Causality, validated by a supermajority consensus algorithm. SPM1D identified significant suprathreshold clusters ([[EQUATION]]), revealing severe kinetic limitations in SLS (peak [[EQUATION]]: 0.67 ± 0.24 Nm/kg; [[EQUATION]]: 5.96 ± 0.89 m/s) compared to AOS (peak [[EQUATION]]: 1.39 ± 0.73 Nm/kg; [[EQUATION]]: 6.41 ± 0.99 m/s), with PWS exhibiting intermediate mechanics (peak [[EQUATION]]: 0.85 ± 0.31 Nm/kg; [[EQUATION]]: 6.15 ± 0.74 m/s). Crucially, dynamic causal modeling revealed a temporally asymmetric, biphasic architecture. The pre-peak acceleration phase exhibited robust ground-driven Bottom-Up dominance ([[EQUATION]]), reflecting anticipatory pelvic anchoring. Following peak velocity (~49–50%), causality strictly inverted to a Top-Down regime ([[EQUATION]]), demonstrating terminal deceleration is an active, effector-guided modulation of ground mechanics. Mechanically restricted stances SLS induced a fragmented causal profile with oscillatory bursts, contrasting with the sustained flow of AOS and the polarized interaction of PWS. These findings establish that ballistic neuromechanics operate as a highly structured, bidirectional causal interplay, providing a rigorous mathematical framework for evaluating kinetic chain integrity.

title: On the Nature of Things: Designing Macroeconomic Scenarios of Naturerelated risks for France
affiliations: Banque de France, Banque de France, Banque de France, Banque de France and Banque de France

detail.title: On the Nature of Things: Designing Macroeconomic Scenarios of Naturerelated risks for France

publicationDetails.detailsText: Banque de France Working Paper No. No. 1046
publicationDetails.journalName: Banque de France Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: This paper explores the macroeconomic implications of nature-related risks for France through a forwardlooking scenario analysis. We first identify and prioritize key nature-related shocks with potential macroeconomic relevance. Using a multi-country semi-structural model, we then design two illustrative scenarios: one focused on water-related shocks-combining chronic scarcity, declining quality, and acute disruptions-and another on agricultural shocks, including domestic yield losses and a multiple breadbasket failure. The simulations suggest that both scenarios generate material impacts on economic activity and inflation in France. Water-related shocks lead to a stagflationary episode marked by a sharp and persistent decline in output and rising prices, while agricultural shocks result in deeper output losses due to global spillovers and food price surges. These findings highlight the macroeconomic relevance of nature-related risks and call for further work on their implications for financial stability.

title: Startups In Africa
affiliations: University of Chicago - Booth School of Business, International Finance Corporations (IFC), World Bank, Columbia University - Columbia Business School, Economics and Stanford University

detail.title: Startups In Africa
detail.abstract: We build new data on startups in Africa to study which types of financing these firms demand, how financing is allocated in practice, and the implications for startup creation and the composition of the sector. We combine a continent-wide founder survey, an incentive-compatible experiment estimating financing preferences, and venture capital (VC) deal records matched to founders' education and work histories. We find that startups strongly prefer equity over debt, but equity is supplied mainly by foreign investors and flows disproportionately to foreign-connected founders. About 80 percent of VC deals involve a foreign investor, and more than 60 percent of funded founders have studied or worked outside Africa. A simple accounting framework shows that this foreignness reflects three main forces: scarce local equity capital, a thin pool of local entrepreneurs able to access startup finance, and frictions limiting local entrepreneurs' access to foreign investors. Together, these forces reduce startup creation and tilt the sector toward foreign investors and foreign-connected founders.

title: Entrepreneurship in Democratic Contexts: Social Contracts, Risks, and Pathways Forward
affiliations: Bruegel

detail.title: Entrepreneurship in Democratic Contexts: Social Contracts, Risks, and Pathways Forward
detail.abstract: In democracies, the interplay between entrepreneurship, democratic values, and societal structures presents profound challenges. These challenges arise from varying social contracts between entrepreneurs and the state across regions, uneven risk distribution that disproportionately affects underserved workers and women, and the glorification of entrepreneurship that often masks reductions in welfare support. These dynamics exacerbate income inequality, particularly in the gig economy, where digital platforms (e.g., Uber and Deliveroo) extract value from precarious workers. Many such workers view themselves as entrepreneurs but frequently earn below minimum wage without adequate protections. The challenge for policymakers then becomes how to encourage innovation and entrepreneurship while adequately protecting entrepreneurs from precarity and promoting equality without compromising democratic values. A promising pathway forward involves cooperatives, which reimagine entrepreneurship as a collective endeavor. By fostering worker ownership and democratic governance, cooperatives mitigate inequality through profit redistribution, enhanced social protections, and democratized technology. This model enables innovation to coexist with robust social support.

title: The Microstructure of Conditional Prediction Markets: A Theory of Selection, Multiplicity, and Mode Collapse in Futarchy

detail.title: The Microstructure of Conditional Prediction Markets: A Theory of Selection, Multiplicity, and Mode Collapse in Futarchy
detail.abstract: We develop a general-equilibrium model of conditional prediction markets organized around a single structural primitive: a belief co-dependence parameter that captures the joint information content of the action and outcome belief channels through the shared latent macroeconomic state. Within-market analysis produces selection bias that grows with this co-dependence, equilibrium multiplicity with saddle-node structure, and a dynamic-stability condition governing whether biases compound across forecasting rounds. The within-market analysis prescribes zero codependence, but this prescription is incomplete: wallet-level transparency on blockchain venues activates a cross-market channel through which a generalized least-squares estimator improves welfare even as bias rises, yielding an interior optimum bounded away from both zero and the temporal-instability threshold. Transparency and sophistication paradoxes further confine the reversal to a narrow interior region that current blockchain venues fall outside.

title: Biased Cupid: Evidence of Prejudice in the US Marriage Market
affiliations: and University of Houston

detail.title: Biased Cupid: Evidence of Prejudice in the US Marriage Market
detail.abstract: This paper studies whether racial prejudice contributes to the persistently low rate of Black-White marriage in the United States. We combine Census and American Community Survey microdata with measures of racial attitudes derived from the General Social Survey and Google search data to examine how local prejudice correlates with interracial matching patterns. To isolate the role of preferences from population composition, we benchmark observed marriage rates against a random-matching counterfactual based on group shares. We document three main findings. First, areas with higher anti-Black prejudice exhibit significantly lower Black-White marriage rates relative to the random-matching benchmark, even after controlling for observable characteristics and segregation. Second, conditional on interracial marriage, Black spouses exhibit stronger observable characteristics-particularly education-consistent with compensating differentials; these patterns are more pronounced in high-prejudice markets. Third, variation in White attitudes toward Blacks is strongly associated with interracial marriage outcomes, whereas variation in Black attitudes toward Whites is not. To interpret these patterns, we estimate a transferable-utility matching model that recovers marriage surplus across partner types. The structural estimates indicate that differences in racial attitudes primarily affect sorting along racial lines. Counterfactual simulations imply that reducing prejudice in high-prejudice areas to the level observed in low-prejudice areas would substantially increase interracial marriage rates. Together, the results suggest that prejudicial preferences play an important role in shaping marriage market outcomes and, more broadly, patterns of social integration.

title: Intraday Microstructure Dynamics of E-mini S&P 500 Futures: Volatility Regimes, Liquidity Decay, and Long Memory in Realized Volatility

detail.title: Intraday Microstructure Dynamics of E-mini S&P 500 Futures: Volatility Regimes, Liquidity Decay, and Long Memory in Realized Volatility
detail.abstract: This paper characterizes the intraday microstructure dynamics of E-mini S&P 500 (ES) futures over 529 trading sessions from April 2024 to May 2026 using one-minute OHLCV data. We document four empirical findings. First, intraday liquidity follows an L-shaped decay: trade activity concentrates at the open and declines monotonically through the session, with mean bar range falling 44% from 4.78 to 2.69 points between the first and last thirty-minute windows. Second, four distinct volatility regimes are identifiedthe April 2025 tariff shock being the most extreme at 33.9% annualized realized volatility, 3.6 times the normal-period mean of 9.3%. Third, realized volatility is strongly persistent: the lag-1 autocorrelation of daily realized volatility is 0.71, with significant positive autocorrelation remaining at lag 21 (one trading month), consistent with long memory. Fourth, mean bar range is a near-sufficient statistic for session realized volatility (Pearson r = 0.975, p < 0.001). These findings validate microstructure signal designs that condition on open-period range expansion, volatility regime state, and persistence before committing to a directional position.

title: Regulating AI in Europe: The EU AI Act
affiliations: University of Newcastle - Law School

detail.title: Regulating AI in Europe: The EU AI Act
detail.abstract: The European Commission released the proposed Regulation on Artificial Intelligence  (the AI Act, hereafter AIA) on 21 April 2021 . The Act was finalised after a relatively swift if heavily lobbied progress on 2 August 2024 .  This chapter lays out the basic structure of the AIA and analyses its origins and controversies around its passing  but also deep dives into important aspects such as whether "AI companions" may be prohibited under art 5, whether the GPAI rules are in the end adequate and what "systemic risk" means if anything.

title: Cooperation without Coercion: A Slack Commitment Rule for the Global Commons

detail.title: Cooperation without Coercion: A Slack Commitment Rule for the Global Commons
detail.abstract: This paper studies whether high-level cooperation in global commons can be sustained without coercion. I introduce a slack commitment rule for a committee subject to a citizen-sovereignty constraint: each participant states the maximum contribution it is willing to undertake, and no obligation may exceed that statement. The rule leaves only a small, rule-based margin between stated willingness and actual commitment, but uses category thresholds to link one participant's statement to the commitments of many others. This creates institutional pivotality in large populations. In a finite-player noncooperative game, I show that, when the population is large and thresholds are set appropriately, full acceptance of the contribution target is the unique Nash equilibrium, while stated willingness is almost fully converted into performance at every profile. The same logic contains exit cascades, supports group-based entry, and provides a recovery path from disequilibrium to cooperative equilibrium.

title: From Artefact to Insight: Efficient Low-Rank Adaptation of BrushNet for Scanning Probe Microscopy Image Restoration
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, Tongji University, National University of Singapore (NUS), affiliation not provided to SSRN and National University of Singapore (NUS)

detail.title: From Artefact to Insight: Efficient Low-Rank Adaptation of BrushNet for Scanning Probe Microscopy Image Restoration
detail.abstract: Scanning Probe Microscopy (SPM) based techniques offer materials characterization at nanoscale resolution but are frequently marred by structured artefacts such as line-scan dropout, gain-induced noise, tip convolution, and phase hops. While most available methods treat SPM artefact removal as isolated denoising or interpolation tasks, the generative inpainting perspective remains largely unexplored. In this work, we introduce a diffusion-based inpainting framework tailored to scientific grayscale imagery. By fine-tuning < 0.2 % of BrushNet weights with rank-constrained low-rank adaptation (LoRA), we adapt a pretrained diffusion model using only 7390 artefact – clean pairs distilled from 739 experimental scans. On our forthcoming public SPM-InpBench benchmark, the LoRA-enhanced model increases the Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (or PSNR) by 6.61 dB and halves the Learned Perceptual Image Patch Similarity or LPIPS relative to zero-shot inference, while matching or slightly surpassing the accuracy of full retraining, trainable on a single GPU instead of four high-memory cards. The approach generalizes across various SPM image channels including height, amplitude and phase, faithfully restores subtle structural details, and suppresses hallucination artefacts inherited from natural-image priors. This lightweight framework enables efficient, scalable recovery of irreplaceable SPM images and paves the way for a broader diffusion-model adoption in nanoscopic imaging analysis.

title: Care Transition Efficiency & Placement Outcome Analytics
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Care Transition Efficiency & Placement Outcome Analytics
detail.abstract: The Unaccompanied Alien Children (UAC) program administered by the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) Office of Refugee Resettlement (ORR) operates as a multi-stage care and reunification pipeline, receiving children from U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) and facilitating their placement with vetted sponsors. While aggregate custody counts are monitored publicly, process efficiency metrics that capture the speed, continuity, and outcome quality of care transitions remain largely absent from published reporting frameworks. This paper presents a systematic, data-driven analysis of the UAC care pipeline using daily operational data spanning January 2023 through December 2025. Five Key Performance Indicators (KPIs) are engineered from the raw dataset: Transfer Efficiency Ratio, Discharge Effectiveness Index, Pipeline Throughput Rate, Backlog Accumulation Rate, and Outcome Stability Score. Temporal analysis, bottleneck detection, and stagnation period identification are applied to characterize system performance across three distinct operational regimes corresponding to different policy environments. Key findings reveal that 393 of 720 reporting days (54.6%) triggered at least one process bottleneck; that all nine detected stagnation periods occurred exclusively in 2025; that total annual sponsor placements fell from 66,244 (2023) to 6,920 (2025), representing a 89.5% decline; and that the 72-hour CBP-to-HHS transfer mandate was systematically breached throughout the second half of 2025. These findings provide actionable insights for policymakers, case managers, and program administrators seeking to improve reunification timelines and child welfare outcomes. These findings are optionalised in an accompanying Streamlit web dashboard enabling real-time interactive exploration of all five KPIs.

title: Private Currency Systems for Large Language Model Companies: A Theoretical Framework for AI Token Economics Based on Trust Mechanisms
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Private Currency Systems for Large Language Model Companies: A Theoretical Framework for AI Token Economics Based on Trust Mechanisms

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflict of interest.

detail.abstract: As the large language model (LLM) industry expands rapidly, a handful of leading AI companies are forming highly sticky digital ecosystems. This paper proposes a novel monetary economics framework: LLM companies issue private digital currencies ("AI Tokens"), whose exchange rates are determined by the market's aggregate trust in the issuing company's technical capabilities and service quality, rather than being pegged to any fiat currency or commodity. Drawing on private currency theory, information asymmetry economics, and digital ecosystem dynamics, we construct a theoretical model examining issuance mechanisms, exchange rate determination, feedback dynamics, and systemic risks. We further propose "AI Trust Index Derivatives" as a transitional alternative that preserves the core informational value of the original concept within existing regulatory frameworks.

title: How Far Does a Climate Shock Travel? Effect of the Panama Canal Disruption on US West Coast Maritime Traffic and Air Pollution
affiliations: University of Southern California - Price School of Public Policy

detail.title: How Far Does a Climate Shock Travel? Effect of the Panama Canal Disruption on US West Coast Maritime Traffic and Air Pollution
detail.abstract: Climate-induced disruptions in global trade routes have significant, far-reaching economic and environmental consequences. This study establishes the causal chain through which a climate shock at a critical chokepoint cascades through the global maritime network to degrade air quality in distant locations. Leveraging the 2023-24 El Niño-induced drought at the Panama Canal as a natural experiment within a chained 2SLS framework, I demonstrate that the disruption did not simply redistribute traffic flow. Instead, it manifested as increased vessel activity at substitute destinations. Especially at US West Coast ports, the arrival of rerouted cargo vessels exceeded port’s operational capacity, causing a significant increase in pre-berthing activity rather than seamless throughput. This increase in maritime activity, in turn, led to a measurable degradation of local air quality. Each additional vessel at West Coast ports increased daily particulate matter (PM1, PM2.5, and PM10) concentrations by 12.6 to 13.3 percent, with the pre-berthing phase generating the largest per-hour effect of 0.54 to 0.57 percent. The findings also reveal notable heterogeneity in how vessel types responded to the disruption. Schedule-constrained cargo vessels rerouted to West Coast ports, generating the observed congestion and pollution increases, while spot-market tankers absorbed the shock without measurable changes in port activity. These results demonstrate that a region's environmental vulnerability depends not only on its direct climate exposure but also on its position within the global maritime network.

title: Monetary Emission: From Stimulus to Financial Extraction: A Structural Deflation Targeting Framework
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Monetary Emission: From Stimulus to Financial Extraction: A Structural Deflation Targeting Framework
detail.abstract: We examine how quantitative easing (QE) transforms from an economic stimulus tool into a mechanism for financial extraction through the Cantillon Effect. Analyzing the distributional consequences of monetary expansion, we find that asset price inflation systematically benefits capital owners while eroding real wages--productivity increased 70% from 1979-2018 while real hourly compensation rose only 12%. We propose the Structural Deflation Targeting (SDT), a framework with declarative debt restructuring tied to technological deflation and redirected emission channels. The model operates through a Master Formula: Distribution mechanisms (75/25 innovator/implementer rule, 70/20/10 with state), and specifications for all seven economic actors. We prove SDT admits stable deflationary equilibria where real wages grow with productivity while maintaining financial stability. Applications include housing (52% price reduction over ten years) and pharmaceutical innovation realignment. The framework includes the Transborder Emission Arbitrage (TEA) Protocol for international implementation and is proven immune to stagflation. Historical validation from 1870-1890 and Moore's Law periods supports feasibility. We validate the framework computationally through three interlocking models: a nine-variable New Keynesian DSGE embedding the Cantillon wedge as a structural state variable -- confirming via forecast error variance decomposition that the Cantillon shock accounts for 45--55% of labour share variance under the standard regime and zero under SDT; a multi-agent simulation operationalising all seven actor roles and four implementation scenarios; and meso-DSGE extensions to the banking sector (NPL -> 0,VaR compressed from 6--8% to 1.2%, reinvestment multiplier confirmed) and to pharmaceutical and renewable energy sectors (resolving the Zero Marginal Cost investment pathology that standard QE cannot address).

title: A Liquidity-Dilution and Effective-Demand Barrier Framework: Monetary Expansion, Asset-Market Sequencing, Purchasing Power Erosion, and the Need for Capital-Accumulation-Oriented Policy
affiliations: Independent Research

detail.title: A Liquidity-Dilution and Effective-Demand Barrier Framework: Monetary Expansion, Asset-Market Sequencing, Purchasing Power Erosion, and the Need for Capital-Accumulation-Oriented Policy
detail.abstract: This paper proposes a liquidity-dilution and Effective-Demand Barrier framework for analyzing how large-scale monetary expansion may generate asymmetric price responses across asset markets and unequal welfare effects across households. The core claim is that liquidity expansion is not transmitted only through the quantity of money; it is also filtered by whether households can convert nominal liquidity into effective demand for capital-preserving assets. The paper begins from the proposition that increases in base money may contribute to broad-money expansion such as M2 through credit creation, banking behavior, regulation, and money demand. When broad money expands relative to the existing money stock, it may dilute the relative value of existing money balances and generate economy-wide nominal price pressure. However, this pressure does not transmit uniformly into consumer prices. Instead, it moves through financial markets, real estate markets, and consumer goods markets according to market accessibility, transaction speed, regulatory friction, behavioral amplification, and effective-demand barriers. A central contribution of this paper is the concept of the Effective-Demand Barrier. Asset prices themselves restrict the number of potential buyers capable of participating in a market. Low-unit-price and highly divisible assets, such as equities, allow broader participation and therefore absorb liquidity faster. By contrast, high-unit-price and less divisible assets, such as real estate, face stronger entry barriers, greater dependence on leverage, and slower transaction adjustment. As a result, liquidity expansion may first produce rapid and amplified responses in financial assets, later transmit into real estate, and finally appear as consumer price inflation. The framework extends the Nominal Pressure Index (NPI) by incorporating asset accessibility, transaction velocity, expectation amplification, regulatory friction, and price-based effective-demand constraints. It then connects these asset-market dynamics to distributional welfare outcomes. Asset-owning households may preserve or increase wealth through asset appreciation, while lower-income and non-asset-owning households often absorb additional liquidity through essential consumption. When asset prices rise before these households can accumulate capital, the barrier to asset ownership increases, and subsequent consumer inflation erodes real purchasing power. The paper concludes that economic policy should not be evaluated solely by short-term consumption support or nominal liquidity injection. Effective policy should simultaneously protect immediate purchasing power and expand long-term capital-accumulation capacity.

title: HAR-RS-DOW Variance Forecasting for Bitcoin: Statistical Dominance and Applications in Risk Management and Option Pricing

detail.title: HAR-RS-DOW Variance Forecasting for Bitcoin: Statistical Dominance and Applications in Risk Management and Option Pricing

detail.abstract: This paper studies the daily realized variance dynamics of Bitcoin (BTC-EUR) over the period April 2019 to May 2026 and establishes the Heterogeneous Autoregressive model with Realized Semivariance and Day-of-Week effects (HAR-RS-DOW) as the statistically dominant variance forecaster for this market. Using realized kernel estimation at five-minute frequency, we estimate ten HAR-family specifications on 2 312 in-sample days and evaluate them out-of-sample over 1 312 days. HAR-RS-DOW dominates the next-best alternative by ΔBIC = 490 in-sample and by 14% lower CRPS out-of-sample, with Diebold-Mariano statistics rejecting equal predictive accuracy against all four nearest competitors at p < 0.005, and the Hansen-Lunde-Nason (2011) Model Confidence Set containing only HAR-RS-DOW at both 90% and 75% confidence levels. The dominance is robust across two robustness dimensions: (i) cross-asset replication on ETH-EUR (n = 2 081) and SOL-EUR (n = 1 738) confirms the BIC ranking and the systematic Saturday day-of-week effect (γ_Sat ∈ [-0.27, -0.19]); and (ii) comparison against the non-HAR benchmark of GARCH(1,1) yields OOS log-realised-kernel R² margins of +0.54 to +0.79 in favour of HAR-RS-DOW across all three assets. We further demonstrate two canonical applications: HAR-driven density forecasts produce conservatively calibrated Expected Shortfall under three density specifications (Acerbi-Szekely Z1 ∈ [+1.73, +2.11]) adequate for Basel III FRTB, and HAR-σ̂ as Black-Scholes input yields fair-value pricing closest to market-clearing. These results support the literature view that realised-measure HAR-family models are optimally deployed as variance forecasters underpinning risk and derivative-pricing applications.

title: When an overexploited resource becomes strategic
affiliations: University of Warsaw - Institute of Applied Mathematics and Copenhagen Business School

detail.title: When an overexploited resource becomes strategic
detail.abstract: We model a situation where a common resource becomes irreplaceable in production of strategic importance, e.g., ofan emergency countermeasure. This happens when the resource is close to depletion and a backstop technology isnot ready. We extensively study a large market based on this common resource. The market consists of many smallfirms producing an intermediate product from the resource, many small firms using this intermediate product as aningredient of a common use product, and several large producers of the countermeasure. We derive an equilibriumof this market. Whenever the resource is close to depletion, “the tragedy of the commons” escalates and the countermeasurebecomes unavailable when the most needed. Nevertheless, crowding out of common-use production turnsout too slow. We also study study the social welfare context and regulations mitigating “the tragedy” for a motivatingexample of shark squalene used in vaccines.

title: Energy-Only Markets and Renewable Deployment: Evidence from ERCOT

detail.title: Energy-Only Markets and Renewable Deployment: Evidence from ERCOT

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is employed as a Load Forecasting Analyst at the Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT). The views expressed are solely the author's own and do not represent ERCOT's official positions. No other competing interests are declared.

detail.abstract: Wind and solar produced an estimated 35--39\% of electricity in the Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT) in 2025, and battery storage reached 13{,}900~MW without a procurement mandate, the largest fleet in the United States. None of this required a clean electricity standard, feed-in tariff, or capacity market.  This paper argues that ERCOT's energy-only wholesale market architecture created institutional preconditions favorable to rapid renewable deployment.  Scarcity pricing rewards low-marginal-cost generators; the \$6.8~billion Competitive Renewable Energy Zone transmission build-out broke a coordination logjam that private capital could not; and federal tax credits underwrote early wind development.  Yet California's mandate-driven model reached comparable wholesale renewable shares, suggesting ERCOT's real edge is speed and cost, not ultimate penetration.  The July~2025 One Big Beautiful Bill Act accelerates the phase-out of wind and solar credits, setting up a natural experiment on whether market signals alone keep capital flowing.  Process-tracing across four causal mechanisms finds evidence consistent with each, though alternative explanations (resource endowment, private land markets, single-state governance) cannot be ruled out.  The same market design that spurred renewables also left the grid exposed during Winter Storm Uri.

title: Labor Adjustment under Demand Uncertainty in Developing Economies: The Role of Operational Levers
affiliations: , University of Cambridge - Cambridge Judge Business School, National Chengchi University (NCCU) - Department of Management Information Systems and INSEAD - Technology and Operations Management

detail.title: Labor Adjustment under Demand Uncertainty in Developing Economies: The Role of Operational Levers
detail.abstract: Manufacturing firms in developing economies face demand uncertainty under institutional conditions that differ from those in developed economies. When demand becomes difficult to predict, firms may adjust not only production, sourcing, or inventory decisions, but also the organizational resources maintained around workers. We examine whether demand uncertainty leads developing-economy manufacturers to compress organizational support resources, whether such compression affects productivity, and which operational levers mitigate these consequences. We use developed economies as an institutional contrast to show that the same demand-side uncertainty can surface through different labor-related channels. Methodology/Results: We construct a global panel of publicly traded manufacturing firms from 2002 to 2024 by combining financial statement, labor-controversy, and buyer-supplier network data. In developing economies, demand uncertainty is associated with lower SG&A expenditure per employee, consistent with organizational support compression, and this channel is also associated with lower productivity per employee, indicating consequences beyond labor-related adjustment. Regional sourcing attenuates the relationship between demand uncertainty and SG&A expenditure per employee, whereas inventory buffers do not. By contrast, in developed economies, demand uncertainty is associated with higher strike incidence, and inventory buffers attenuate this relationship. Instrumental-variable estimates support these patterns. Managerial Implications: Our findings show that managing demand uncertainty requires operational levers that fit the institutional channel. In developing economies, preserving organizational support under demand uncertainty may require responsiveness-based levers, such as regional sourcing, rather than slack-based inventory buffers. Because support compression is associated with lower productivity, such levers may help protect both laborrelated resources and productive capability. By contrast, inventory buffers appear more relevant for attenuating labor tensions in developed economies. More broadly, the study cautions against directly transferring operational prescriptions from developed-economy contexts to developing-economy settings.

detail.title: Monetary Tightening, Global Liquidity Fragmentation, and Asset Repricing in Emerging vs Developed Markets
detail.abstract: This paper examines how monetary tightening in advanced economies affects asset pricing across emerging and developed markets under fragmented global liquidity. Using SVARs, panel regressions, time-varying parameters, and regime-switching models, we find that tightening leads to orderly, valuation-based adjustments in developed markets, but causes larger, more persistent, and state-dependent repricing in emerging markets. These asymmetries intensify during periods of liquidity fragmentation, highlighting risk-premium and balance-sheet channels, and posing implications for global financial stability.

title: Sangīta, Sacred and Shared: Protecting Sri Lanka’s Traditional Music in the Digital Age

detail.title: Sangīta, Sacred and Shared: Protecting Sri Lanka’s Traditional Music in the Digital Age
detail.abstract: Sri Lanka, often described as the "Teardrop of India," is a country where the heartbeat of the land is echoed in its music. Sinhala folk music, or Sangīta, flows through daily rituals, seasonal work, and sacred ceremonies, carried in the voices of poets, drummers, and dancers across generations. From the lyrical beauty of kavi (poetic verses) and seepada (quatrains) to the vibrant rhythms of Geta Bera and the stylised chants of Vannam, these traditions form a vital part of the island's cultural identity. Yet in the digital era, this living heritage is increasingly vulnerable. Traditional music, once protected by ritual and community, now circulates online without consent, attribution, or legal safeguards. The Intellectual Property (IP) Act No. 36 of 2003 includes only limited references to folklore and lacks the tools needed to address collective ownership, community consent, or misuse through digital platforms. This article examines the current gaps in protecting traditional music in Sri Lanka and explores comparative approaches adopted in countries such as India, South Africa, and Peru. It argues for the urgent need for a sui generis legal framework, community-based rights mechanisms, and digital-era protections to ensure that these sacred and shared expressions of culture are respected, safeguarded, and rightfully attributed to their source communities. Ultimately, it identifies that protecting Sangīta is not only a question of legal reform but a call to preserve the soul of a nation.

detail.abstract:
Background: Civil registration systems in many low- and middle-income countries capture only a fraction of vital events, with deaths recorded less completely than births. Globally, female deaths are more often unregistered, yet evidence from Kenya is lacking. We examined gender bias in adult death registration across three Kenyan Health and Demographic Surveillance System (HDSS) sites.

Methods: We conducted a cross-sectional household survey of 1,363 households reporting a recent death (2022–2023) across three HDSS sites in Nairobi, Kisumu, and Kilifi. Mixed-effects logistic regression identified determinants of registration, and Fairlie decomposition quantified the gender gap. Reported reasons for (non)registration were also analysed.

Findings: Among 1,111 adult deaths, registration was 22·8% overall and significantly higher in males than females (26·1% vs 18·8%; p=0·006). Among females, registration odds were higher in those aged 45–64 than 65–84 years (AOR 2·32; p=0·019) and in Muslims (AOR 2·53; p=0·042), and lower in the unemployed (AOR 0·43; p=0·004). Among males, odds were lower for single individuals (AOR 0·30; p=0·012) and home deaths (AOR 0·64; p=0·048), and higher with employment or retirement (AOR 2·16; p=0·001) and greater wealth. Observable factors, principally economic activity and place of death, explained 50·2% of the 7·4 percentage-point gender gap. Inheritance needs and social benefits motivated registration; low awareness, perceived low benefit, and cost were key barriers.

Interpretation: Gender bias in adult death registration persists in Kenya, driven by socioeconomic and structural barriers that disadvantage women, underscoring the need for gender-responsive civil registration and vital statistics reforms.

title: Reverse Sanctions Evasion: The Case of Russian Oil Re-exports to the European Union via Georgia

detail.title: Reverse Sanctions Evasion: The Case of Russian Oil Re-exports to the European Union via Georgia
detail.abstract: This paper examines reverse sanctions evasion by analyzing how Russian oil and petroleum products subject to EU and G7 restrictions are redistributed through third countries. Using Georgia as a case study, it extends sanctions evasion theory beyond the conventional Sender-to-Target paradigm by introducing a Target-to-Sender trade configuration in global energy markets. Drawing on monthly trade data for petroleum products (HS 2710) from January 2018 to June 2025, the study applies a difference-indifferences (DiD) framework to evaluate trade adjustments following the March 2022 oil sanctions. Results show that Georgia's imports of Russian petroleum products increased significantly relative to other suppliers, indicating trade redirection toward intermediary economies. Export responses occur primarily through prices rather than quantities, with revenues shifting toward non-coalition markets under the price cap regime. The findings reveal a structural vulnerability of energy sanctions, whereby intermediary jurisdictions facilitate indirect circulation of sanctioned commodities within formally legal trade structures.

detail.abstract: The European Green Deal and comparable national climate strategies invest heavily in cobenefit communication-the argument that fighting climate change boosts jobs and economic competitiveness. But does this framing activate or suppress individual climate action? Using Standard Eurobarometer 83.4 (May-June 2015, 27 EU member states, N = 23,556), collected before the Paris Agreement and the European Green Deal, this paper finds no supporting evidence for the assumption that co-benefit beliefs stimulate individual action. Using Poisson and negative binomial count models alongside a structural equation model (SEM), the paper documents a consistent negative association: green growth belief is associated with fewer personal climate actions (𝑃𝑜𝑖𝑠𝑠𝑜𝑛: 𝑏 =-0.118, 𝑝 < 0.001; SEM direct effect: 𝑏 =-0.381, 𝑝 < 0.001), even after controlling for environmental concern. The SEM further reveals that green growth beliefs are negatively associated with environmental concern (𝑏 =-0.897, 𝑝 < 0.001), which in turn positively predicts action (𝑏 = 0.057, 𝑝 < 0.001). The indirect pathway accounts for a portion of the total negative effect. These findings are consistent with a techno-optimism substitution hypothesis: individuals believing systemic solutions will deliver climate action may reduce their own behavioral engagement. Results are robust across distributional assumptions. The pre-Paris Agreement setting ensures estimates reflect genuine attitudinal heterogeneity rather than institutional messaging effects. These findings should be interpreted as behavioral associations rather than evidence of causal displacement. Rather than challenging the validity of co-benefit communication strategies, this paper aims to refine understanding of their behavioral implications.

detail.title: AI in Criminal Justice: Why Governance Matters and How to Make it Work

publicationDetails.detailsText: Stanford Law School Law and Policy Lab, 2025 Fall

detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly embedding itself into the core machinery of the criminal justice system, powering everyday decisions from police analysis of digital evidence and pattern detection in crime data to prosecutorial discovery management, charging recommendations, algorithmic risk assessments in courts, and large language models for summarizing records and drafting documents. These tools promise efficiency gains—processing vast data volumes, reducing backlogs, and optimizing scarce resources in an overburdened system—but they also carry profound risks: embedding bias, producing opaque or unreliable outputs, shifting unmonitored power to vendors, and influencing high-stakes liberty decisions like arrests, detention, sentencing, and release. The central problem is that AI capabilities are deploying without sufficient understanding of their mechanics, failure modes, or implications for constitutional rights, democratic accountability, and system legitimacy. Criminal-justice entities who encounter AI tools—thousands of under-resourced police departments, prosecutors’ offices, courts, and probation units—lack the technical expertise to evaluate these tools rigorously, while vendors market directly to practitioners. This creates a governance gap: even well-intentioned actors cannot reliably apply emerging standards amid rapid technological changes, risking uneven, superficial oversight that undermines public trust.

detail.abstract: The mammalian brain's default response to prolonged, inescapable stress is not a learned failure of motivation, but an evolutionarily hardwired state of metabolic energy conservation. Historically, clinical frameworks addressing depression, chronic trauma, and behavioral passivity have been anchored in the behavioral premise of "learned helplessness"-the theory that organisms actively compute a cognitive expectation of powerlessness. A major neurobiological paradigm shift has inverted this foundational assumption, demonstrating that behavioral passivity under prolonged stress is an unconditioned, automatic survival mechanism mediated by the hyperactivation of serotonergic neurons in the midbrain dorsal raphe nucleus (DRN). True resilience relies on an active, top-down cognitive process mediated by the ventromedial prefrontal cortex (vmPFC) that tracks behavioral-environmental contingencies to inhibit this default brainstem freeze response. This synthesis reorients the clinical paradigm from "unlearning helplessness" to "actively training controllability." It provides a neurobiologically grounded, operational framework for structuring micro-contingency loops in Behavioral Activation (BA), executing cognitive attributional realignment in Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT), and sequencing interventions within trauma-informed care.
