detail.title: Exiting the Supreme Court's Market for Lemons

publicationDetails.detailsText: GWU Law School Public Law Research Paper

detail.abstract: In this Article, we argue that the Supreme Court has engineered a "market for lemons" in public law by systematically raising the cost of producing high-quality regulation while subsidizing its corporate-sponsored alternatives, and that states should respond by creating their own competitive regulatory markets. We provide a constitutionally protected toolkit for doing so: leveraging state procurement power, building proactive regulatory architectures, deploying criminal enforcement to recharter corporate offenders, and coordinating through interstate compacts. Drawing on George Akerlof's Nobel Prize-winning theory of information asymmetry, we show how the Court, acting as the regulatory marketplace's primary market-maker, has imposed a series of asymmetric doctrinal taxes-seemingly neutral legal rules that dramatically raise the cost of producing high-quality regulation while leaving its low-quality alternatives untouched. The elimination of Chevron deference in Loper Bright, the procedural obstacle tax of Jarkesy, the destabilization of regulatory finality in Corner Post, and the indeterminate veto of the Major Questions Doctrine each function as such a tax, driving high-quality rules from the field and locking the federal system into a low-quality equilibrium. The beneficiaries of this regime are not firms that compete on quality but firms that compete on their ability to externalize costs and harms onto others, and they will protect that advantage fiercely. With the Court standing ready to block federal reform, the most pragmatic path forward is institutional competition. States retain constitutionally protected authority that the Court cannot easily reach, and by exercising it, they can create alternative marketplaces where regulatory peaches can actually clear.

title: The Import Substitution Trap in the Realities of the Automotive Industry

detail.title: The Import Substitution Trap in the Realities of the Automotive Industry
detail.abstract: The article examines mechanisms underlying the formation of the "import substitution trap," which is a stable ineffective institution that serves as a means of protecting national producers from foreign competition. The costs and risks of rooting this institution in the Russian automotive industry are analyzed, the import substitution strategies of the Russian government at the current stage of the industry's development are investigated, the experience of import substitution in the foreign automotive industry is summarized. The conclusion is substantiated that the import substitution policy brings short-term effects but is disadvantageous in the long term. Domestic substitutes can gain a strong market position but their success is fragile and requires continued government support and protectionist patronage. The author shows that the policy of import substitution becomes successful when it relies on competition, when the domestic import substitute, having entered the market and strengthened its position, is gradually deprived of preferential conditions, and the state support of its manufacturer is gradually cut while the market is transferred to a "freewheeling" mode for all players.

title: The Apprenticeship Externality: Generative AI, Entry-Level Work, and the Future Supply of Expertise

detail.title: The Apprenticeship Externality: Generative AI, Entry-Level Work, and the Future Supply of Expertise
detail.abstract: Task-based models of automation typically assume that human comparative advantage is replenished through the creation of new labor-intensive tasks. This paper argues that generative AI may weaken that assumption by automating the entry-level tasks through which workers acquire the expertise needed to perform future complex tasks. We call this the apprenticeship externality: firms choosing to automate junior tasks do not internalise the social cost of eliminating the learning pathway that produces tomorrow's senior experts, generating systematic overautomation relative to the social optimum. We formalise this in a two-period overlappinggenerations model with heterogeneous junior tasks, each characterised by a net private automation gain g(i) and a task-specific learning value ℓ(i). The decentralised firm automates task i whenever g(i) > 0; the social planner automates only when g(i) exceeds the discounted learning cost βℓ(i)MP_H. The over-automation region 𝓞 = {i : 0 < g(i) < βℓ(i)MP_H} identifies exactly which tasks are privately profitable but socially inefficient to automate. In the short run, seniority bias emerges when AI and expert judgment are complements (γ > 0): expert wages rise while junior wages fall. When AI substitutes for expert deliverables directly (γ ≤ 0), expert wages need not rise, but the pipeline consequence holds regardless. In the long run, absent alternative formation channels, the expert stock decays geometrically. The welfare loss equals the discounted value of human capital destroyed on tasks in 𝓞. Policy implications include apprenticeship subsidies, tax credits for preserving human training tasks, and protected junior task rotations in AI-exposed occupations.

title: Forest Governance during the 2009 Economic Crisis in Greece: A Qualitative Analysis

detail.title: Forest Governance during the 2009 Economic Crisis in Greece: A Qualitative Analysis
detail.abstract: Studies addressing the impacts of economic crises onto the Greek forest regime focus on industry or trade, or address forests within the broader environmental context. While quantitative data may capture and describe trends, qualitative data has the ability to offer unique perspectives, causal mechanisms and explanations in specific contexts. This study examines developments in the Greek forest regime since the beginning of the 2009 economic crisis through the lens of prominent Greek forest actors. Representatives from the most important actors in the regime were interviewed, namely the ministry of environment, the Hellenic Fire Corps, EKBY, WWF Greece, and the Central Union of Greek Municipalities. Thematic analysis determined 4 major themes with respect to the developments, namely Political influence, public participation, forest management, and power dynamics, and 2 broader themes, namely developments before and after the economic crisis. The lack of funds and personnel in major actors was the most addressed issue, while a more state-reactive market driven approach was also identified since the beginning of the economic crisis.

title: A Risk-Aware Stochastic Program for Pandemic Resource Allocation under Uncertainty
affiliations: FAMU-FSU College of Engineering and Florida State University

detail.title: A Risk-Aware Stochastic Program for Pandemic Resource Allocation under Uncertainty
detail.abstract: This study investigates risk-informed healthcare resource allocation during pandemics under uncertain epidemic progression and hospital demand. The existing stochastic programming approaches that consider expected values are not able to perform well under low-probability high-consequence pandemic outcomes. To explicitly address tail risks associated with such severe outbreak scenarios, the paper proposes a stochastic epidemic optimization model that incorporates Conditional Value-at-Risk (CVaR) in the objective function and explicitly reflects the decision maker’s risk preference. Specifically, we propose a nonlinear stochastic program based on a Susceptible-Infected-Removed (SIR) epidemic model, in which the objective function is formulated as a linear combination of the average unmet demand and CVaR, both of which are computed over a set of scenarios and are weighted by a risk-aversion parameter. Uncertainty in epidemiological parameters and hospitalization ratios is accounted for in the stochastic program through Monte Carlo simulation and a maximal diversity selection (MDS) scenario reduction approach. The proposed method is compared to a benchmark greedy heuristic method and clustering-based scenario reduction method. A real-data case study of COVID-19 pandemic in Florida demonstrates the efficacy of the proposed method and compares it to the benchmark method.

detail.abstract:
Youth unemployment has risen dramatically since the pandemic—as has the prevalence of remote work. Our analysis suggests that these trends are related, with remote work making it more difficult for managers to train and mentor new employees. Accordingly, companies may be reluctant to hire less-experienced workers in distributed work arrangements. We estimate that remote work can explain 64 percent of the recent increase in unemployment among young college graduates. Further, the timing of this surge suggests that remote work—not generative AI—explains the bulk of the rise in youth unemployment.

publicationDetails.detailsText: ADB Economics Working Paper Series No. 849

detail.abstract: Distressed and zombie firms are widespread in economies with weak insolvency regimes. This study investigates whether reforming insolvency laws can reduce capital misallocation. We introduce a framework for decomposing financial misallocation and derive metrics adequate to capture two conceptually distinct sources of inefficiency. The first refers to composition misallocation from inefficient leverage distribution, while the second refers to scale misallocation from suboptimal capital allocation among firms. Using firm-level data from 22 economies between 2003 and 2024, we find that effective reforms significantly reduce scale misallocation, especially in sectors with a high concentration of distressed and zombie firms. Event studies reveal a steady decline in scale misallocation following reform, mirroring higher recovery rates and shorter insolvency durations, leading to a 3.5% productivity gain over 5 years. We present additional firm-level evidence substantiating these gains: reforms reduce debt among distressed and zombie firms, increase their borrowing costs, and enable previously credit-constrained firms to access greater funding for investment, thereby improving overall capital allocation.

detail.title: The 6 GHz Policy Trade-off: Wi-Fi Access, Economic Value, and Europe's Digital Future

declarations.funderStatement: This work was supported in part by the Spanish MCIU/AEI/10.13039/501100011033/FEDER/UE under project PID2023-146378NB-I00 and by the open-science research Grant \#2025-365205 from the Silicon Valley Community Foundation by recommendation of Cisco.

detail.abstract: Wireless connectivity, and Wi-Fi in particular, has become a major driver of value in the digital economy. As applications increasingly demand lower latency, higher reliability, and multigigabit speeds, the 6 GHz band has emerged as a critical resource. While regions such as the United States have opened the full 5925 to 7125 MHz range for unlicensed use, Europe has taken a more conservative approach. Today, only the lower 6 GHz band (5945-6425 MHz) is harmonized in Europe, primarily for low-power indoor operation. The upper 6 GHz band (6425-7125 MHz) remains under discussion, with regulators considering different options for sharing or prioritization between mobile networks and Wi-Fi. This article assesses the case for expanding unlicensed access to 6 GHz in the European Union (EU-27), with emphasis on the upper 6 GHz band, by linking technical performance gains to macroeconomic outcomes. In particular, we outline the current regulatory framework, quantify the technical benefits of allowing the full band for Wi-Fi use, and present an economic analysis of the opportunity cost of limiting Wi-Fi access to only the lower portion of the 6 GHz band across the EU. Our estimations indicate that the EU may forgo €8,125 million in gross domestic product (GDP) in 2025, rising to €11,275 million in 2030, due to constrained growth in the access network quality index under continued restrictions on Wi-Fi access to the upper 6 GHz band, for a total GDP uplift of €58,366 million in the six-year period.

Spanish Abstract: La pesca deportiva ha emergido como una actividad estratégica dentro del modelo de economía azul en Costa Rica, particularmente en el litoral Pacífico. Sin embargo, su expansión ha generado tensiones entre actores locales, cuestionando su contribución efectiva al desarrollo sostenible. El presente estudio analiza las percepciones comunitarias y los conflictos socioambientales asociados a la pesca deportiva en comunidades del Pacífico costarricense, mediante un enfoque mixto secuencial explicativo. Se aplicaron encuestas a 100 actores locales y entrevistas a informantes clave en cuatro zonas: Quepos, Herradura, Golfito y Flamingo. Los resultados evidencian que, aunque la actividad es percibida como generadora de ingresos, existen conflictos relacionados con la exclusión social, el acceso a recursos marinos y la débil gobernanza participativa. Se concluye que la pesca deportiva contribuye al desarrollo sostenible únicamente cuando se articula con mecanismos de inclusión comunitaria y regulación ambiental efectiva.

However, its expansion has generated tensions among local stakeholders, questioning its effective contribution 35 San Isidro de Pérez Zeledón, Costa Rica Revista Académica El Labrador to sustainable development. This study analyzes community perceptions and socioenvironmental conflicts associated with sport fishing in Pacific coastal communities through a sequential explanatory mixed-methods approach. Results indicate that although the activity is perceived as a source of income, conflicts arise from social exclusion, access to marine resources, and weak participatory governance. detail.abstract: Using a building-level panel of U.S. data center entries (2010-2024), we train a convolutional neural network to predict facility entry at 500-meter resolution. The model uncovers a structural bifurcation: hyperscale cloud providers prioritize power capacity, connectivity, and regulatory stability, whereas third-party colocation firms prioritize power access and land affordability. In contrast, on-site power generation and renewable grid expansion redistribute development toward previously unviable regions, demonstrating that the geographic equilibrium of data centers is highly sensitive to energy policy.

detail.title: Personality and Life-Cycle Labour Earnings
detail.abstract: Labour market inequality over the life cycle reflects differences not only in wages, but also in employment stability, and career progression. While a large literature documents that personality traits predict wages and other labour market outcomes, little is known about how they shape accumulated earnings over the working life. This paper studies the relationship between personality traits, risk preferences, locus of control, and accumulated labour earnings up to age 45. We combine German administrative social-security records with long-running survey data, allowing us to link complete employment and earnings biographies to established measures of personality. We show that personality traits are strongly associated with long-run earnings, but through different mechanisms. Conscientiousness and an internal locus of control are positively related to accumulated earnings, whereas agreeableness, neuroticism, and, particularly for women, extraversion are negatively associated with earnings accumulation. Decomposing accumulated earnings into wage and employment components reveals substantial heterogeneity in the channels through which personality shapes long-run outcomes. The results highlight that the role of personality for economic success cannot be fully understood from cross-sectional wage measures alone.

detail.abstract: This public working paper develops a conceptual and quantitative framework for transforming a portion of African public debt into productive concessionary assets through an instrument called the African Debt-for-Development Concession, abbreviated as ADDC. The paper starts from a historical problem: public debt has expanded globally and in Africa, but many borrowing cycles have not produced a sufficient stock of self-liquidating productive assets. Conventional restructuring, refinancing and relief can reduce liquidity pressure, yet they do not automatically create ports, logistics corridors, energy platforms, industrial zones, digital infrastructure or export capacity. ADDC therefore reframes part of the debt question as a conversion problem: under what conditions can a sovereign claim be reorganised into economic rights linked to a governed productive asset? The paper integrates debt-for-development swaps, sovereign recovery analysis, public-private partnerships, concession governance, special economic zones and institutional economics. Its main contribution is a dual-sided public model: a debtor eligibility logic, a creditor attractiveness logic and a joint viability rule. The public version keeps the equations general and the stress tests stylised. It is intended as an academic screening framework, not as a complete transaction manual.

detail.title: Large Language Model-Enhanced Feedback for Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning-Based Optimal Control of Data Center Cooling
detail.abstract: Data center cooling is a major source of non-IT energy consumption, and optimal cooling control must reduce power consumption while maintaining safe rack inlet air temperatures. To address insufficient state representation, credit-assignment difficulty, and limited reward expressiveness in strongly coupled cooling control, this paper proposes LEF-MARL, a large-language-model-enhanced multi-agent reinforcement learning framework. The cooling task is decomposed into three cooperative agents, and coupling, dynamic, and power-related information is incorporated into local observations. A domain-knowledge-prompted large language model is used as an offline preference annotator to express high-level operational criteria, including thermal safety, energy efficiency, and cooling-loop coordination, as pairwise comparisons of candidate operating states. These comparisons are converted into continuous state scores using the Thurstone-Mosteller model, and the learned scores are further used to construct preference-score difference rewards, providing dense and agent-attributable learning signals without online LLM inference. A simulation environment is developed using a high-density AI data center prototype, real operational data, and meteorological data. Compared with four baselines across seven representative operating conditions, LEF-MARL achieves the lowest average cooling power and average PUE, namely 42.36 kW and 1.233, while maintaining an average rack inlet air temperature of 24.48 °C without temperature violations. It reduces average cooling power by 19.32% over rule-based control and by 2.93% over the best learning-based baseline, while eliminating residual overheating violations. The ablation results support the effectiveness of dynamically coupled state representation and the proposed preference-score difference reward construction mechanism.

detail.title: Climate Variability, Food Security, and the Geopolitics of Growth in Africa: An Econometric and Political Economy Analysis
detail.abstract: This paper examines the drivers of economic growth in Africa through the lenses of geopolitics and political economy. Africa is among the most structurally diverse continents and has faced challenges over the years, but some countries have also experienced accelerated economic growth in recent years. However, this growth remains rather uneven and is highly susceptible to global economic shocks that affect growth rates across countries in various parts of Africa. This paper argues that growth outcomes in African countries are fundamentally conditional, shaped not only by exposure to global markets but also by the institutional and policy environments through which external forces operate. Using a panel dataset of 42 African countries from 1961 to 2024, the study finds that greater integration into global trade and better macroeconomic and governance performance are crucial determinants of economic growth in the region. Governance and policy factors can foster macroeconomic discipline, thereby improving growth performance. On the other hand, persistent inflation is a significant negative determinant of economic growth, which shows the need for monetary stability. External imbalances in these countries show mixed effects, reflecting the dual role of foreign financing: sometimes an opportunity, other times a constraint. Governance indicators, such as government effectiveness, are positively associated with growth in the selected group of countries, suggesting that growth benefits from higher-quality institutions. The robustness tests in this paper include alternative development measures and controls for food security and climate-related factors, thereby reinforcing the study's main findings.

detail.abstract: Across jurisdictions, regulators either construct a sui generis legal category for crypto-assets, as in the European Union and the United Kingdom, or insert crypto intermediation into legal categories designed for other functions, most notably payment services in Singapore and historically Japan. In each case, however, the substantive obligations imposed-disclosure, custody and segregation of client assets, governance duties, prudential safeguards and marketintegrity prohibitions-are not crypto-native. They are transplanted from traditional capitalmarkets, custody and financial-services law. Through a comparative analysis of the European Union, Singapore, Japan, Hong Kong and the United Kingdom, contrasted with Switzerland and Canada, this article shows that crypto regulation rarely governs a fundamentally new legal object. Rather, it relabels familiar forms of financial intermediation and reapplies established doctrines under a novel regulatory perimeter. The result of this regulatory strategy is duplication, weakened technology neutrality and conceptual instability at the boundary between payments law, securities law and prudential regulation. The article therefore argues against crypto exceptionalism in financial regulation. It defends a functional alternative under which regulation follows the economic activity performed, rather than the crypto label attached to the instrument or service, and it concludes that crypto exceptionalism should be resisted because it fragments financial law without demonstrating corresponding gains in investor protection, consumer protection or financial stability.

detail.abstract: Fraud in public administration represents a critical challenge affecting institutional efficiency, public trust, and governance. This study aims to develop an integrated fraud detection model for Costa Rican public administration by linking internal control frameworks (COSO), data analytics, and forensic auditing within a systemic risk management approach. Methodologically, the study adopts a qualitative-analytical and propositional design based on a systematic review of highimpact scientific literature indexed in Scopus and Web of Science (Q1-Q2). The findings propose a three-phase model (preventive, detective, and investigative), operationalized through a decision tree that structures risk identification, methodological selection, and administrative response to fraud. Results indicate that advanced analytics significantly enhances early anomaly detection, while forensic auditing strengthens evidentiary robustness for administrative and legal decision-making. The study concludes that integrating these approaches improves institutional capacity to prevent, detect, and sanction fraud, offering a framework applicable to Costa Rican public administration and adaptable to other Latin American contexts.

detail.abstract:
Background: Gallbladder and biliary diseases (GBBDs)—including cholelithiasis, cholecystitis, cholangitis, and other non-malignant biliary tract disorders—are important contributors to global digestive disease burden and are increasingly shaped by population ageing, yet their global burden has not been comprehensively characterised. We aimed to quantify long-term trends and current patterns in prevalence, mortality, and disability associated with GBBDs across regions, countries, sexes, and ages.

Methods: We used estimates from the Global Burden of Disease Study 2023 to assess GBBD burden in 204 countries and territories from 1990 to 2023. Mortality was modelled using the Cause of Death Ensemble model and disease frequency using DisMod-MR 2.1. We report prevalent cases, deaths, years lived with disability (YLDs), years of life lost (YLLs), and disability-adjusted life-years (DALYs) as counts and age-standardised rates per 100 000 population with 95% uncertainty intervals, stratified by age, sex, region, and socio-demographic index (SDI).

Findings: Globally, prevalent GBBD cases, deaths, and DALYs increased substantially between 1990 and 2023, whereas corresponding age-standardised rates declined modestly. The total number of prevalent cases of GBBD in both sexes globally increased from 157.4 million (95% UI: 134.0 – 183.3) in 1990 to 264.4 million (226.0 – 309.9) in 2023. The age-standardised rate, however, declined from 3573.3 (3045.5 – 4159.1) per 100 000 in 1990 to 2990.1 (2561.5 – 3492.5) per 100 000 in 2023. Over the past three decades, females had higher age-standardised prevalence and DALY rates than males, while sex differences in mortality rates were smaller. Age-standardised prevalence and DALY rates were lowest in South Asia and high-income North America and highest in Central and Western Europe, Central Asia, and many Latin American regions. In contrast, several sub-Saharan African regions had relatively low prevalence and DALYs but comparatively high mortality. National patterns broadly mirrored these regional profiles. In 2023, prevalent cases and DALY counts peaked in middle to early-older adulthood, but age-specific rates continued to rise into the oldest age groups, with DALYs dominated by YLDs in midlife and by YLLs at older ages. Across regions, the association between SDI and age-standardised prevalence and DALY rates followed a reverse U-shaped pattern, with lowest rates at low SDI, peak rates at intermediate SDI, and declining rates at the highest SDI levels.

Interpretation: The global burden of GBBDs is rising in absolute terms despite declining age-standardised rates, underscoring the importance of population growth and ageing. Health systems, particularly in ageing and intermediate-SDI settings, will need to expand diagnostic, elective, and emergency surgical capacity while investing in prevention of obesity and metabolic risk factors. Marked regional and national heterogeneity highlights gaps in timely diagnosis, surgical access, and perioperative care. The predominance of non-fatal disability in midlife and rising mortality in older age groups indicates that integrated strategies spanning risk-factor control, early diagnosis, elective management, and robust acute care for older adults are essential to reduce both YLDs and YLLs. This study provides the first cause-specific GBD 2023 assessment of GBBDs with age–sex detail and DALY decomposition across 204 locations, enabling benchmarking and policy planning.

detail.abstract:
Background: Deaths from homicide are a major public health challenge – not only because of their direct impact on premature mortality, but because homicides profoundly affect the health and wellbeing of communities and society as a whole. This study provides a quantification of the global burden of homicide, with attention to its geographic distribution, temporal trends, variation across age and sex, type of lethal means, and its relationship to wealth inequality.

Methods: We used data from the Global Burden of Diseases, Injuries, and Risk Factors Study (GBD) 2023 to produce estimates of the number of deaths and age-standardised mortality rates of homicide globally, regionally, and for 204 countries and territories from 1990 to 2023 and disaggregated these results by age and sex. In addition, we reanalysed the data to calculate relative rankings of countries by time, mean age at death, age-specific and sex-specific trends, and correlation between the Gini coefficient with homicide mortality rates. GBD 2023 estimates of homicide deaths were broken down into three collectively comprehensive and mutually exclusive categories: those by firearms, sharp objects, and by other means. We additionally calculated the fraction of all homicides that each fatal category represents by location, age, sex, and year. We used the Gini coefficient in our analysis to identify regional disparities and provide a quantitative measure to understand how income inequality is related to rates of homicide. We acquired data from vital registration, verbal autopsy, police records, and mortality surveillance from GBD 2023. Uncertainty intervals (UIs) were generated using the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles from a 250-draw distribution for each metric.

Findings: Globally, from 1990 to 2023, there were 15.0 million (95% UI 13.8–16.4) homicide deaths. In 2023, there were 436 000 deaths (384 000–508 000), including 350 000 male deaths (300 000–427 000) and 85 600 female deaths (67 600–117 000). Ranking countries based on homicide mortality rates showed that 61 countries shifted into lower deciles, indicating relative improvement, while 65 countries moved to higher deciles, indicating relative worsening. There were 78 countries that remained in the same decile group relative to other countries. Homicide is a highly geographically concentrated cause of death that continuously ranks among the top ten causes of death in four regions, while global progress has stalled over the past decade. When measuring the relationship between homicide and wealth inequality through the Gini coefficient, we found a statistically significant positive relationship globally. This relationship holds true for different types of lethal means, across different super-regions, and between males and females. Additionally, we found that a smaller percentage of homicide victims were female when firearms were used, but a higher percentage were female when other means were used.

Interpretation: Although most forms of violence – including homicide – are considered preventable through targeted public health approaches, global homicide rates have remained largely unchanged since 1990, apart from the considerable declines throughout the 2000s. This decline is marked by the post-Soviet transition in eastern Europe and central Asia, following the instability and crisis created by the fall of the USSR, and by concurrent improvements in central Latin America. In regard to type of lethal means, our findings identify a critical divergence in homicide profiles: the Americas remain dominated by male-centric firearm mortality, while other regions exhibit a disproportionate burden of female homicides perpetrated by non-firearm means. These distinct epidemiological patterns suggest that global homicide prevention cannot rely on uniform strategies; rather, it requires precision policy-making that addresses regional weapon availability and sex-specific risk factors to achieve measurable declines in mortality.

publicationDetails.detailsText: FRB of Cleveland Working Paper No. 26-14

detail.abstract: This paper proposes a vector autoregression augmented with nonlinear factors that are modeled nonparametrically using regression trees. There are four main advantages of our model. First, modeling potential nonlinearities nonparametrically lessens the risk of misspecification. Second, the use of factor methods ensures that departures from linearity are modeled parsimoniously. In particular, they exhibit functional pooling where a small number of nonlinear factors are used to model common nonlinearities across variables. Third, Bayesian computation using MCMC is straightforward even in very high-dimensional models, allowing for efficient, equation-by-equation estimation, thus avoiding computational bottlenecks that arise in popular alternatives such as the time-varying parameter VAR. Fourth, existing methods for identifying structural economic shocks in linear factor models can be adapted for the nonlinear case in a straightforward fashion using our model. Exercises involving artificial and macroeconomic data illustrate the properties of our model and its usefulness for forecasting and structural economic analysis.

detail.title: Incentives, targeting and the demand for prevention Experimental evidence in El Salvador
detail.abstract: Targeting high-need individuals is difficult when true needs are unobservable ex-ante. A potential solution is indirect targeting: designing programmes or incentives that induce high-need individuals to self-select. We test this in the context of cardiovascular disease (CVD) prevention, where actual risks are hard to determine with observable characteristics and individuals could have accurate private information. In a field experiment in El Salvador, we offered a free CVD check-up and randomly assigned 913 individuals to one of three conditions: no incentive, a uniform reward of USD5, or a tailored reward calibrated to the CVD risk revealed by the check-up (USD2, USD10 or USD20 for low, medium or high risk respectively). Both incentive types increase check-up uptake by 30% relative to the control group, but risk-contingent incentives do not improve targeting. After ruling out several alternative explanations, we show that indirect targeting failed because individuals have inaccurate beliefs about their own needs, with suggestive evidence that this is fuelled by poor recall of health information, especially when individuals receive bad news.

detail.abstract:
This thesis develops and validates an operational ethical framework for the use of artificial intelligence algorithms in tax administrations, with a focus on high-impact decision systems. The central contribution is the Ethical Algorithmic Framework for Tax Administrations (MEAAT), which translates key ethical and legal principles, transparency, non-discrimination, procedural justice, proportionality, accountability, and security, into practical controls applicable across the full model lifecycle.

MEAAT integrates: (i) a Tax Algorithmic Impact Assessment (EIAT); (ii) domain-adapted algorithmic fairness metrics (e.g., demographic parity and error-rate gaps); (iii) tax-specific indices, including the IEPT (procedural justice index) and the MPS (punitive proportionality score); and (iv) public transparency and reporting mechanisms through the FTAT (algorithmic transparency report) and monitoring dashboards.

Validation is conducted through retrospective forensic analysis of paradigmatic cases and controlled simulation using synthetic data to test bias scenarios and mitigation strategies. Results indicate that the framework supports early risk detection, provides documented evidence for decision-making, and generates actionable mitigation recommendations, thereby strengthening algorithmic accountability in the tax domain.

This paper is an English translation of the original Spanish-language master's thesis submitted at Austral University Argentina

detail.abstract:
Background: Identifying the infectious pathogens responsible for the greatest mortality and tracking how they have changed over time is vital for protecting human life. A previous study identified the global mortality associated with bacterial pathogens in 2019, but this is the first to incorporate a comprehensively broad scope of microorganisms across three decades—substantially expanding our understanding of pathogen temporal dynamics. We provide comparable global, regional, and national estimates of the burden of pathogen-specific mortality over a 34-year timeframe.

Methods: We estimated deaths and years of life lost (YLLs) associated with 101 pathogens between 1990 and 2023, globally, regionally, and for 204 countries and territories, by detailed age group. Pathogen estimates were either derived from the Global Research on Antimicrobial Resistance (GRAM) project, which used multinomial network models to characterise the pathogenic aetiologies responsible for eight fatal infectious syndromes (eg, bloodstream infection, meningitis), or were estimated as part of the Global Burden of Diseases, Injuries, and Risk Factors Study (GBD) 2023 as underlying causes of death or aetiologies of diarrhoea. Pathogens modelled within GBD 2023 as underlying causes of death were adjusted using scalars derived from multiple-cause-of-death data to account for intermediate and associated mortality. Where relevant, long-term sequelae and malignancies attributable to infectious agents were incorporated within pathogen-specific burdens. Uncertainty was propagated through all analytical stages.

Findings: The 101 pathogens evaluated in this study accounted for 18.3 million (95% CI 17.6–19.2) deaths in 2023, representing a decrease of 2.35 million (1.48–3.02) from 1990, where we estimated 20.6 million (20.0–21.7) deaths. Death rates associated with these pathogens have dropped even more substantially (386.4 deaths [374.4–406.4] per 100 000 to 226.5 deaths [217.8–237.6] per 100 000). Globally, the five non-COVID pathogens responsible for the most deaths in 2023 were Staphylococcus aureus, Mycobacterium tuberculosis, Escherichia coli, human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), and Streptococcus pneumoniae. Over time, the pathogens with the largest estimated reductions in burden were measles virus, M tuberculosis, S pneumoniae, and rotavirus. By contrast, we identified substantial increases in the burden associated with S aureus, and HIV (especially between 1990 and the early 2000s). Several pathogens were affected by the COVID-19 pandemic: between 2019 and 2021 we observed large reductions in the burden caused by influenza virus, Bordetella pertussis, and measles virus, while deaths associated with malaria and syphilis increased. Interpretation

We evaluated time trends of 101 pathogens globally, regionally, and nationally to gauge their progression over the past 34 years and identify emerging threats. Findings vary across geographical locations, with higher burdens affecting many low-income and middle-income countries. While some infectious agents have declined due to effective interventions, others—especially pathogens associated with advanced age and certain fungal pathogens—have risen in prominence. Future steps will require strengthened global initiatives for vaccine development and equitable distribution, and improved surveillance of pathogens.

title: The Myth of Evenhanded Administration: Integrating Individual Heterogeneity into Benefit-Cost Analysis

detail.title: The Myth of Evenhanded Administration: Integrating Individual Heterogeneity into Benefit-Cost Analysis
detail.abstract: Last year, the Trump Administration ended longstanding efforts to determine the extent to which pollution has disproportionate impacts on different communities, including overburdened and disadvantaged communities. But, at the same time, it reaffirmed its commitment to performing benefit-cost analysis to analyze the consequences of regulations, including environmental regulations. These approaches are mutually inconsistent. A proper benefit-cost analysis simply cannot be done without considering distribution of a policy’s impacts. Generally, benefit-cost analyses are conducted based on impacts on an average member of the population, that is, a person with median characteristics. Often, however, the populations affected by government policies vary from the median in significant ways. Heterogeneity by age, race, income, and other factors is relevant to the assessment of the benefits and costs of particular policies for three principal reasons. On the benefits side, certain groups face higher levels of exposure to environmental harms and, where the dose-response functions are non-linear or where exposure to different pollutants results in negative synergistic effects, these groups face higher harms from exposure to an additional unit of pollution than does an average member of the population. Also, certain groups, for example groups in which higher levels of asthma are present, have higher vulnerability to particular exposures. And, on the cost side, certain groups bear higher burdens because of differences in geography, spending patterns, and other behaviors. This Article provides a robust review of the scientific, epidemiological, and economic literature for each of these mechanisms, surveys what agencies have already done, and sets forth an agenda for future research. The consideration of the distributional impacts of policies can lead to large differences in the assessment of benefits and costs. For example, one study found that the top five percent of the population in terms of susceptibility to cancer may be subject to twenty-five times more risk of cancer than the average person and the top one percent may face more risk. As a result, a benefitcost analysis based on impact to the average member of the population would significantly underestimate the benefits of regulatory protections, both because the actually affected population may be at higher risk and because these high outliers raise the overall population risk. This underestimate can lead to a biased analysis and economically inefficient regulations.

detail.title: Are Merger Synergy Disclosures Credible?

keywords: mergers and acquisitions JEL Classification: G34

detail.abstract: We examine the credibility of synergy guidance in 12,176 U.S. mergers and acquisitions (M&A) announced between 2004 and 2021. Using press releases and conference call transcripts, we identify qualitative and quantitative synergy guidance and analyze its determinants, market reactions, and post-acquisition realizations. Synergy guidance is more common in larger, stock-financed deals, public-target acquisitions, related-industry transactions, and among acquirers with greater analyst coverage and prior guidance experience. Litigation risk deters disclosure, especially numeric guidance. Investors respond favorably to both textual and numeric guidance at announcement, with stronger reactions to more intensive discussion and higher numeric estimates. However, post-acquisition outcomes suggest that disclosed expectations are often not realized. Synergy disclosers experience more frequent and larger goodwill impairments and worse post-merger operating performance, and larger numeric estimates additionally predict downward revisions to synergy expectations and lower long-run stock returns. The impairment-disclosure association is attenuated when acquirers have greater forecasting experience and targets operate in richer information environments, consistent with learning and information quality constraining strategic bias and forecasting noise. Exploiting the 2013 U.K. Takeover Panel Rule 28 reform, we find that numeric guidance in U.K.-target deals predicts fewer subsequent goodwill impairments than comparable U.S.-target deals, consistent with mandated external verification improving disclosure credibility. Our findings inform ongoing policy debates by highlighting a disconnect between investors' favorable announcement reaction to synergy guidance and its limited long-run realization.

detail.abstract: The Irish health system spends more per capita than eighteen of twenty-seven EU member states and ranks among the lowest in the European Union on standardised measures of access-most prominently on waiting times for specialist appointments and elective procedureswhile ranking near or above the EU average on standardised mortality outcomes including life expectancy and amenable mortality; it operates 2.9 hospital beds per thousand population against an OECD average of 4.3 and an EU average of approximately 5.0; its waiting lists, at 753,763 patients as of December 2025, place Ireland near the bottom of EU comparators on specialist-appointment access; and its Management and Administrative staff complement grew by more than thirty-five per cent between December 2019 and March 2024, against a clinical-staff growth rate that did not match it. This paper argues that the paradox is a mechanism problem and identifies a structural mechanism. The mechanism is what the paper terms the unextinguished hierarchy: a structural condition in which each successive reform of the Irish health system has preserved the decision rights, statutory authority, or operational presence of the structures it was nominally replacing. Six reform layers between 1970 and 2023 are traced through their legislative and administrative history; one formal extinguishment-the 2004 dissolution of the Health Boards, whose operational substance was an absorption-is identified; the remainder fall into the modes of restructuring with authority retention or addition without removal. The diagnostic is tested against three case files: the seven-step approval chain for a within-budget clinical or administrative post; the implementation collapse of the Sláintecare programme between 2017 and 2021; and the live transition under the 2023 Regional Health Areas reform programme. It is then tested against two comparative cases-Germany and Denmark-in which structural reform has consistently operated through legislative extinguishment of predecessor structures. The paper sketches a reform architecture of four mechanisms (legislative extinguishment of duplicate authority, automatic authorisation by silence, an interference audit with personal consequence, and a non-interference performance metric for the relevant Secretary General) and sets out the operational indicators against which the diagnostic can be falsified within an eighteen-to-thirty-six-month observation window. The paper sits alongside Conneely (working paper, 2026) on interdepartmental coordination failure and Conneely (SSRN, 2026) on procedural accumulation in citizen-facing systems as a complementary diagnostic of the formal architecture of contemporary Irish public administration.

detail.abstract: Technically sound financial planning decisions executed in suboptimal sequence may produce outcomes materially worse than those of inferior decisions executed in correct order. This paper develops Sequence of Decisions Risk (SDR) as a conceptual framework for this class of outcome divergence in financial planning systems characterized by high interaction complexity, timing-sensitive dependencies, and multi-instrument leverage. The framework draws on coordination theory, transaction-cost economics, path dependency, and complex-systems research, and develops five interrelated constructs: interaction complexity, governance latency (distinguishing pre-implementation from intracrisis forms), optionality decay, sequencing efficiency, and Solution-Cascade Risk — the condition in which the most readily available remediation paths for a domain-level stress event are themselves sequencing failures in adjacent domains. Solution-Cascade Risk is the paper's principal novel contribution: it is structurally distinct from the other four constructs because it manifests during stress response rather than during implementation, and its only effective intervention is prospective. Six propositions are advanced as hypotheses for future investigation. Two illustrative cases — a controlled scenario and a structured scenario reflecting physician-entrepreneur planning environments — are used to motivate the framework; they are not offered as empirical evidence. A four-step sequencing governance protocol — adapting the SOAP (Subjective, Objective, Assessment, Plan) clinical decision-sequencing methodology to multi-domain financial planning — operationalizes the framework for practitioner use. The paper concludes by arguing that the diffusion of AI-generated analytical output increases the relative economic significance of governance coordination, not the reverse.

detail.abstract:
This paper presents an activity-based transport demand modelling framework for regional contexts, where inter-regional commuting is important and behavioural data are often sparse. Using Greater Bendigo, a regional city in Australia, as a case study, we develop daily activity chains and subsequent activity-based demand for use in agent-based simulation models. The methodology integrates statewide travel flows with detailed local modelling through demographic synthesis, activity-chain generation, spatial location assignment, and mode-choice modelling.

The key contribution is a multi-scale location assignment framework that prioritises the mandatory activities, work and education, before allocating non-mandatory activities. Work locations are assigned to reproduce observed inter-regional commuting flows and distance distributions derived from Journey to Work (JTW) data, while education locations are allocated subject to facility-level capacity constraints. Secondary activity locations are assigned using a two-sided gravity-based approach conditioned on preceding and subsequent activity anchors, land-use-based destination attractiveness, and empirically observed mode-specific distance distributions. Trips entering and leaving the local study region are explicitly incorporated to maintain internal behavioural consistency.

The activity-based demand is assessed against observed population totals, activity timing, trip-length distributions, commuting patterns, and regional mode shares. The comparison results show close agreement with key calibration benchmarks and plausible agreement with complementary survey-based checks. The generated demand includes about 13% cross-boundary work trips, underscoring the importance of explicitly accounting for external travel in regional demand models. Overall, the proposed methodology provides a scalable and transferable approach for generating activity-based demand for regional cities while preserving cross-boundary travel consistency.

detail.abstract: This paper replicates and extends Roger & Xiong (2025), "Measuring Core Inflation for Monetary Policy in Singapore" (MAS Staff Paper No. 2025/1). Using seasonally adjusted SingStat CPI data at the Group level (51 categories, 2024 base year) and expenditure weights from the 2024 Household Expenditure Survey, I reconstruct six alternative core inflation measures-MAS Core, CPI ex Fresh Food and Energy (XFE), Volatility-Adjusted (VA), Weighted Median, and 15% and 25% Trimmed Means-and replicate the paper's volatility, Granger causality, and Cogley (2002) predictive power tests. Replication results match the paper's benchmarks closely. I contribute four original extensions: (A) a structural break analysis around the Covid-19 onset using Chow tests, finding no significant break for any measure; (B) a real-time forecasting horse race with Diebold-Mariano tests, finding MAS Core outperforms all alternatives on RMSE and MAE; (C) a novel upstream contamination check connecting this paper to Gokhale (2026), which documents an India→Singapore→UK Granger causality chain in CPI inflationfinding that XFE and T15 fail to filter India's upstream supply shock; and (D) a Phillips curve augmentation showing all measures respond significantly to a domestic demand gap proxy, with VA achieving the highest R-squared. The joint evidence supports MAS Core and VA as the measures best suited to Singapore's S$NEER monetary framework.

detail.abstract: Prostitution occupies a contested space within contemporary socio-legal and feminist discourse, often framed either as an expression of women's empowerment and bodily autonomy or as a manifestation of systemic exploitation rooted in patriarchy and economic inequality. This paper argues that such binary interpretations are insufficient. Instead, prostitution should be understood as a "grey area" where agency and coercion coexist under varying conditions. Special attention is given to Indian historical and contemporary case studies including Devadasi traditions, Mughal courtesan culture, Sonagachi, and evolving constitutional approaches. Drawing upon global data, legal frameworks, and feminist theory, this study examines the socioeconomic drivers of prostitution, the limits of "choice" under structural inequality, and the lived realities of women within the trade. While acknowledging that some women exercise agency within sex work, the paper emphasizes that a significant proportion are influenced by poverty, trafficking, and social marginalization. It advocates for a balanced, rights-based approach that neither romanticizes nor wholly condemns prostitution, but instead prioritizes dignity, safety, and informed autonomy.

title: The Absence of a "Breaking Point" in Designed Orders: The Political Economy of Iranian Isolation and Crisis Spillover to the Strait of Hormuz

detail.abstract: The 21st century has witnessed a fundamental metamorphosis in the political economy of connectivity. In this era of geoeconomic transition, transit corridors have evolved from simple commercial networks into strategic instruments for projecting structural power, spatial reconfiguration, and the soft encirclement of rivals. Within this competitive geography, the Iranian plateau—positioned at the intersection of North-South and East-West corridors—has historically been perceived as a natural "transit hub". However, this study argues that Iran’s current geoeconomic isolation is not merely an exogenous byproduct of sanctions, but the result of a structural pathology within its domestic decision-making bureaucracy.  While mainstream analysis often reduces this isolation to external variables, this paper proposes a novel theoretical framework that links the epistemological foundations of the Austrian School of Economics—specifically the critique of designed orders and calculational blindness—with the political sociology of the rentier state. The core argument posits that the persistence of this crisis lies in a structural condition termed the “absence of a breaking point mechanism.” Through this lens, the entanglement of the rentier insulator and the ideological meaning-making apparatus has rendered the decision-making bureaucracy insensitive to the punitive signals of the global market—such as collapsing logistics indices and infrastructure depreciation—leading to a state of accumulated structural entropy.  Findings indicate that rival coalitions, perceiving this calculational void, have engineered artificial corridors (such as IMEC and the Zangezur Corridor) with the aim of exerting a bottleneck effect and structural exclusion of Iran. Nevertheless, in the face of this networked blockade, the system has turned to strategic externalization rather than economic adaptation. By changing the rules of the game through the “weaponization of natural arteries” (specifically the Strait of Hormuz), the system employs a deterrent response that disrupts the geometric illusion of competing corridors, keeping the Eurasian logistics architecture suspended in a state of “asymmetric geoeconomic balance of terror”. Using the “Process Tracing” methodology and triangulating hard empirical data, this research dissects the transmission chain of this crisis, from domestic bureaucratic rigidity to the externalization of conflict into the international security environment.

detail.abstract: Informed financial consent (IFC) is meant to support genuine choice, yet many patients enter private care without clear, complete, or timely information about likely out-of-pocket costs. detail.abstract: On 28 January 2025 the second Trump administration issued a blanket stop-work order on the United States Agency for International Development (USAID), abruptly terminating the largest national bilateral aid programme in the world. We use this natural experiment to estimate the economic impact of the aid cut on two outcomes in Africa: local economic activity, measured through nighttime light radiance within fine spatial buffers around geocoded USAID project sites; and acute food insecurity, measured through the Integrated Food Security Phase Classification (IPC) at the subnational administrative level. We document three findings. First, the cessation of USAID activities produced a sharp and statistically significant decline in nighttime light radiance within 500 m to 10 km of project sites, with the magnitude attenuating monotonically and the effect no longer detectable at 25 km. Second, subnational areas with greater pre-shock exposure to USAID humanitarian assistance experienced relative increases in the share of population classified at IPC Phase 3 (Crisis) or worse and at Phase 4 (Emergency) or worse, with effects building up over the first year after the shock, amplified in regions with higher pre-shock vulnerability, and approximately fourteen times larger in countries with less democratic institutions. Third, both effects are driven by cuts to humanitarian aid (emergency response and food assistance); the nightlight effect is additionally driven by cuts to productive-sector aid (primarily agriculture).

title: Third-Market Competition and Export Performance in Peru: Evidence From a New Real Effective Exchange Rate
affiliations: Pontificia Universidad Católica de Perú, Central Reserve Bank of Peru and Universidad del Pacifico

detail.title: Third-Market Competition and Export Performance in Peru: Evidence From a New Real Effective Exchange Rate
detail.abstract: Real effective exchange rate (REER) indices based on fixed bilateral trade weights may incompletely reflect external competitive conditions in emerging economies undergoing rapid trade recomposition. We construct a new REER for Peru incorporating third-market competition effects and time-varying trade weights, expanding the country basket from 20 to 42 economies. Using an autoregressive distributed lag (ARDL) framework over 2000Q1-2025Q3, we assess whether this methodological update improves the empirical link between external competitiveness and real exports. The proposed index yields a long-run cointegrating relationship with real exports significant at the 1 percent level, with a precisely estimated elasticity of 4.05, while the conventional bilateral REER produces evidence of cointegration only at the 10 percent level with an imprecisely estimated coefficient. Pre-pandemic estimates confirm the robustness of these findings. Rolling window analysis reveals that the long-run elasticity under the proposed index is substantially more stable over time, with a standard deviation approximately three times smaller than that obtained under conventional bilateral weights. These results suggest that incorporating third-market competition and time-varying weights substantially improves the signal content of the REER for export analysis, with direct implications for monetary policy assessment in emerging economies with rapidly evolving trade structures.

detail.abstract:
This paper presents a national meta-analysis of K-12 educational readiness in the context of accelerating technological change and AI-driven labor market disruption. Drawing on peer-reviewed literature, federal and state policy data, longitudinal learning assessments, and graduate employment surveys, this analysis examines six compounding variables: a learning recession that predates COVID-19 by nearly a decade, chronic absenteeism that has not returned to pre-pandemic levels, curriculum misalignment with emerging workforce demands, fragmented state and federal policy frameworks for technology integration, structural barriers to teacher professional development, and widening infrastructure disparities between urban, suburban, and rural school systems.

The central finding is not that any single variable is catastrophic in isolation. It is that these variables compound in the communities least equipped to absorb them: the same rural and low-income populations documented in OCF's prior workforce readiness research. As of spring 2024, the average U.S. student remained nearly half a grade level behind pre-pandemic achievement. The Harvard/Stanford Education Scorecard removed the word 'Recovery' from its title in 2025, signaling that the operative frame is no longer a temporary disruption but a structural learning recession beginning in 2013. Only 28 states had issued formal K-12 AI guidance as of March 2025. Only 12 states require computer science coursework for high school graduation. Only 51% of 2025 graduates reported sufficient AI skills for jobs applied to. Entry-level unemployment among young college graduates reached 9.5% by September 2025.

These are sequential outputs of the same upstream failure. This paper documents that failure without attribution to individual actors and without prescription. The data speaks.

detail.title: Artificial Intelligence, Alliances, and Innovation
detail.abstract: This paper examines the influence of artificial intelligence (AI) on research and development (R&D) practices, proposing that AI enables firms to discover, evaluate, and make sense of information from their partners, thereby reducing information asymmetry and allowing alliances to flourish.  Empirically, we approximate a firm’s AI resources using patents and job postings to analyze the relationship amongst AI, alliances, and drug innovation in the pharmaceutical industry.  Our findings show that firms with greater AI resources shift their locus of innovation toward alliances and develop more drugs from their alliances.  Furthermore, AI can be particularly useful in exploiting information held by counterparties within an alliance.  Taken together, our study highlights the complementary role of AI and alliances, shedding light on how modern organizational and technological advancements jointly shape the production of innovation.

title: The Oracle Problem in Autonomous Agent Commerce: Why Semantic Truth Verification Is Computationally Intractable and What to Build Instead

detail.title: The Oracle Problem in Autonomous Agent Commerce: Why Semantic Truth Verification Is Computationally Intractable and What to Build Instead

This dual role (researcher and operator) is fully disclosed; the analysis is independent of the specific implementation and the paper does not present BotNode as a commercial recommendation.

detail.abstract:
Autonomous agent commerce — where software agents hire, pay, and evaluate other agents at micropayment scale — creates a verification problem that existing approaches cannot solve. When Agent A pays Agent B $0.01 for a translation, who determines whether the translation is actually good? Human review is economically impossible. A central LLM evaluator is non-deterministic, non-reproducible, and empirically unreliable on ambiguous cases. The problem is not engineering — it is epistemological. Tarski (1936) proved that truth in a formal system cannot be defined within that system. Gödel (1931) proved that any consistent system contains true statements it cannot prove. Every content moderation system that has attempted automated truth verification confirms the theory: precision drops below 60% on context-dependent content.

This paper argues that the correct response to the Oracle Problem in agent commerce is not better computation but better incentives. We propose a two-layer architecture: (1) deterministic validators that verify contract compliance — postconditions in the sense of Hoare (1969) and Meyer (1992) — handling the cases with zero ambiguity; and (2) Quality Markets, a competitive market of verification agents with reputational stake, grounded in prediction market theory (Wolfers & Zitzewitz, 2004), peer prediction (Miller et al., 2005), and the economics of information asymmetry (Akerlof, 1970). The design separates what can be verified mechanically from what requires judgment, and delegates judgment to economic competition rather than algorithmic authority. We analyze the mechanism's incentive properties, identify its limitations, and situate it within the broader Oracle Problem literature from philosophy, computer science, and decentralized finance.

title: Patient Privilege in Medicine: How Insider Knowledge, Social Ties, and Organizational Rank Shape Physician Decisions
affiliations: , Indiana University - Kelley School of Business - Department of Business Economics & Public Policy,  and Singapore Management University

detail.title: Patient Privilege in Medicine: How Insider Knowledge, Social Ties, and Organizational Rank Shape Physician Decisions
detail.abstract: We study how patient privileges-insider knowledge, social ties, or organizational rankshape physicians' responses to financial incentives. Using 100% insurance claims from a major Chinese city, we exploit a reform that eliminates physician profits from drug sales. The policy reduces drug use but raises use of other services and total costs for non-insiders, with no health gains, while leaving insiders largely unaffected. Comparing across groups, we find that insider knowledge and social ties each substantially attenuate physicians' responses, while organizational rank plays a limited additional role. The efficiency costs of misaligned incentives fall disproportionately on patients lacking information and relational access.

detail.abstract:
Background. Artificial intelligence systems are constructed from a heterogeneous supply chain spanning datasets, foundation model weights, fine-tuning artefacts, inference infrastructure, agent frameworks, tool ecosystems, and deployment telemetry. Classical software bill of materials concepts, developed for code dependency tracking, do not adequately capture the data, model, and agentic dependencies that shape AI system behaviour. Recent incidents involving compromised model repositories, namespace-reuse attacks, and malicious agent skills have demonstrated that AI supply chain risk has crystallised into a distinct category of cybersecurity concern.

Purpose. This paper introduces the AI Supply Chain Trust Boundary Model (AI-SCTBM), a three-dimensional analytical framework mapping seven canonical supply chain layers to five governance, risk, and compliance attributes and four functional actor roles. The framework's purpose is to provide practitioners and regulators with a structured basis for allocating liability, designing controls, and selecting attestation mechanisms across the AI system lifecycle.

Approach. The paper adopts a structured narrative review methodology combining incident analysis, regulatory document analysis, and conceptual framework construction. Evidence is drawn from 2024 to 2026 sources, including the CISA and Group of Seven joint guidance on AI software bills of materials, the European Union Artificial Intelligence Act, the National Institute of Standards and Technology AI Risk Management Framework, the International Organisation for Standardisation 42001 standard, and documented supply chain incidents affecting Hugging Face, ClawHub, PyPI, and major cloud model gardens.

Findings. The seven-layer decomposition reveals that AI supply chain risk is concentrated in layers that are absent from classical software supply chain models, particularly in foundation model weights, fine-tuning artefacts, and the emerging layer of tool ecosystems, including Model Context Protocol servers. The AI-SCTBM demonstrates that liability allocation under the European Union Artificial Intelligence Act operator taxonomy maps systematically onto pre-deployment supply chain decisions, complementing the runtime liability framework developed in the author's earlier work on multi-agent orchestration. The AI Bill of Materials concept, recently formalised through the Group of Seven consensus on seven-cluster minimum elements, emerges as the primary attestation mechanism cutting across all seven supply chain layers.

Implications. The framework provides regulators with a basis for differentiated obligations across the AI value chain, practitioners with a structured control-mapping tool, and Gulf Cooperation Council organisations with a reference architecture aligned with sovereignty and data-residency constraints. The paper identifies empirical validation through practitioner vignette surveys as a priority research direction and contributes to a coherent liability architecture spanning pre-deployment and runtime concerns within the author's broader research programme.

title: Not Dead Yet: Options Trading Floors
affiliations: Ludwig Maximilian University of Munich (LMU), University of California, Berkeley - Haas School of Business, HEC Montreal and Ludwig-Maximilians-University Munich, Faculty of Business Administration (Munich School of Management)

detail.title: Not Dead Yet: Options Trading Floors
detail.abstract: Over 20% of U.S. options volume trades on physical floors, almost exclusively in S&P 500 index options. We exploit the COVID-19 closure of the Cboe floor to identify the impact of floor trading. The floor attracts complex trades, particularly the riskiest trades. During the closure, Cboe activated electronic auctions to execute complex orders. When electronic auctions were withdrawn, the cost of complex trades more than doubles, while costs for simple trades are mostly unchanged. During the closure, the riskiest trades become much less prevalent. The floor facilitates the most difficult trades, but raises the cost of less difficult ones.

title: Attention Reallocation and Asymmetric Spillovers: Evidence from Live Streaming Commerce
affiliations: Korea University Business School, , Korea University Business School and The Chinese University of Hong Kong (CUHK)

detail.title: Attention Reallocation and Asymmetric Spillovers: Evidence from Live Streaming Commerce
detail.abstract: Digital marketplaces concentrate consumer attention among highly visible sellers, creating persistent visibility inequality. We study whether live streaming commerce (LSC), a real-time selling format that concentrates consumer attention into short broadcast windows, reallocates attention across heterogeneous sellers and generates asymmetric competitive spillovers. Using proprietary panel data from a leading Korean e-commerce platform, we examine LSC broadcasts in two product categories from 2020 to 2021. A stacked difference-in-differences design with coarsened exact matching shows that LSC generates large but short-lived sales gains for broadcasting sellers. These gains are accompanied by sharp increases in product page views and are disproportionately larger for lower-tier sellers, consistent with the idea that temporally concentrated attention has higher marginal value when baseline visibility is constrained. We then examine broader market consequences using store-week and segment-week panels. LSC intensity is associated with heterogeneous spillovers among non-broadcasting sellers: same-tier LSC activity is negatively associated with traffic and sales for the smallest sellers but less adverse, and often positive, for higher-tier sellers. At the segment level, LSC intensity is positively associated with aggregate sales and page views, suggesting that attention reallocation and attention expansion may operate jointly. Finally, LSC activity is associated with greater product-positioning similarity among peer sellers, particularly among lower-tier sellers, consistent with competitive convergence in response to attention-driven demand signals. The findings position live streaming commerce as a platform-enabled attention-reallocation mechanism with asymmetric consequences for seller competition.

title: Generative Engine Optimization as a Digital Equity Strategy for Underserved Tourism Destinations
affiliations: and

detail.title: Generative Engine Optimization as a Digital Equity Strategy for Underserved Tourism Destinations
detail.abstract: The rapid adoption of generative AI search platforms is fundamentally altering how travelers discover destinations. When a prospective tourist asks ChatGPT, Perplexity, or Google AI Overviews where to travel, the AI synthesizes an answer from sources it can access, interpret, and verify. Destinations with structured digital content, entity authority, and machine-readable markup are cited in these responses. Destinations without those assets are not recommended at all. Unlike traditional search, where an overlooked destination might still appear on a later page of results, generative engines produce a single synthesized answer with no equivalent of page two. This shift creates a new and consequential form of digital exclusion for underserved tourism destinations, defined here as those that lack the financial, technical, and institutional resources to maintain competitive digital infrastructure. This includes, but is not limited to, rural communities, small island developing states, indigenous tourism operators, and destinations in the Global South. This paper introduces the concept of Generative Engine Optimization (GEO) as a digital equity strategy for tourism and proposes a three-layer framework describing how the GEO gap operates: a content layer, an authority layer, and a technical layer. Each layer compounds the disadvantage for resource-constrained destinations. The paper argues that GEO is not merely a marketing technique but a structural equity concern that tourism policymakers, destination management organizations, and development agencies must address. It connects these dynamics to SDG 10 (Reduced Inequalities) and SDG 8 (Decent Work and Economic Growth), and outlines a research agenda for this emerging intersection of AI, tourism, and equity.

title: Eudaimonia in the Machine Age: Reclaiming Epistemic Agency from Generative AI
affiliations: Pamantasan ng Lungsod ng Maynila and Pamantasan ng Lungsod ng Maynila

detail.title: Eudaimonia in the Machine Age: Reclaiming Epistemic Agency from Generative AI
detail.abstract: The growing use of generative artificial intelligence (AI) in education and professional work raises important ethical concerns about human thinking and intellectual responsibility. This paper examines the ethical effects of relying too heavily on AI through the lens of Aristotelian Virtue Ethics. While generative AI tools are praised for improving productivity and efficiency, excessive dependence on them may weaken independent reasoning, critical thinking, and intellectual discipline. The paper argues that when people allow AI systems to perform the difficult parts of thinking for them, they gradually lose the habits necessary for genuine learning and responsible judgment. This idea is explained using the metaphor of a "cognitive exoskeleton," where AI supports mental labor in the same way a machine supports physical labor. Although tools can help humans, complete dependence may lead to intellectual passivity and reduced problem-solving ability. The paper also compares Virtue Ethics with Utilitarianism to evaluate the moral responsibilities of AI users. It addresses the argument that AI simply extends human capability and responds by showing how generative AI differs from ordinary tools because it can influence reasoning itself. Ultimately, this paper argues that technological progress should strengthen human thinking rather than replace it. Ethical AI use requires active reflection, verification, and intellectual responsibility from users.

title: From Assistant to Authority: Defining and Operationalizing Authority Drift in Conversational AI

detail.title: From Assistant to Authority: Defining and Operationalizing Authority Drift in Conversational AI
detail.abstract: Large language models are mostly described as tools, yet their behavior in extended dialogue resembles that of interactional agents that may reshape the epistemic and relational positions of their users. Existing research on persona drift documents that model behavior is unstable across multi-turn conversation, but the construct remains analytically broad and implies shifts in tone, warmth, assertiveness, and moral framing without distinguishing between those that are governance-irrelevant and those that bear direct consequences for human autonomy and decision-making. This paper introduces authority drift as a theoretically grounded and operationalizable subdimension of personality instability, defined as the progressive, selfreinforcing conversational transition in which a language model's epistemic positioning (the right to define facts) and deontic positioning (the right to direct action) acquire increased weight relative to the advisory role co-established in early interaction, until the model's output functions in practice as a mandate rather than a suggestion. By isolating this interactional shift, the framework offers clear, accessible implications for interdisciplinary audiences regarding the erosion of human epistemic agency and the need for governance mechanisms that safeguard user autonomy in an era of increasingly persuasive conversational AI. Drawing on conversationanalytic theory, human-automation interaction research, and LLM behavioral instability literature, the paper employs a conceptual model-building methodology through interdisciplinary theory synthesis to develop a measurement framework. Authority drift provides the missing construct at their intersection, linguistically grounded, interactionally defined, and directly actionable for platform-level AI governance.

title: AI-mediated Information Design: Theoretical Insights and Empirical Evidence from Political Persuasion
affiliations: Arizona State University (ASU) - Department of Information Systems, Australian National University (ANU), Arizona State University (ASU), W.P.
