detail.title: AI-mediated Information Design: Theoretical Insights and Empirical Evidence from Political Persuasion
detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) increasingly mediates how information is consumed through automated summaries and interactive conversational agents. This raises a fundamental question for information design: how does switching to an AImediated information environment change the responsiveness of beliefs to information, and how would strategic senders (e.g., firms, media, politicians) optimally disclose information when messages are mediated through AI? In this paper, we develop an information design framework in which the receiver's responsiveness to information depends on the communication technology through which information is consumed, allowing systematic deviations from Bayesian updating. We test the framework using an artefactual field experiment in a U.S. presidential election context, where voters receive news through traditional articles, AI-generated summaries, or AI chatbots. The AI-mediated conditions hold informational content fixed to isolate the effect of communication technology on belief updating. We find that AI-mediated interfaces (especially conversational agents) substantially reduce responsiveness to informational signals and increase reliance on prior beliefs. We embed these estimated technology-specific belief response functions into our information design model and show that reduced responsiveness fundamentally reshapes optimal disclosure. Specifically, when receivers are less responsive and relying more on prior beliefs, optimal strategies involve more informative disclosure. More generally, our theory implies that technologies reinforcing prior beliefs polarize optimal strategies: senders must provide more informative signals to skeptics but can rely on less informative disclosure for supporters. Further, while AI-mediated audiences can induce more informative disclosure overall, heterogeneous AI adoption can generate asymmetric belief responses across adopters and non-adopters, potentially amplifying polarization. Our findings inform media organizations, platform designers, and policymakers about how AI-mediated interfaces can reshape the effectiveness and consequences of strategic communication.

title: The ACP Model: Operational Authority Drift in AI-enabled Industrial Systems
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: The ACP Model: Operational Authority Drift in AI-enabled Industrial Systems
detail.abstract: AI systems are making consequential operational decisions in bulk electric systems, water treatment facilities, and industrial process environments. When those systems degrade, through concept drift, deployment-context mismatch, or data integrity failure, existing frameworks do not model how that degradation propagates through operational decision layers into physical consequence. This paper presents the AI Consequence Propagation (ACP) Model: a five-stage sociotechnical propagation model for AI-enabled industrial systems. Unlike static hazard causality frameworks, ACP models adaptive AI-mediated dependency propagation, where the propagation mechanism is not a fixed system property but an emergent behavioral condition that develops after deployment. The model introduces operational authority drift: a condition in which operational dependency on AI outputs exceeds formally authorized decision boundaries without any explicit system reconfiguration. ACP treats this drift as a central propagation mechanism linking AI reliability degradation to physical consequence. A detailed scenario applies the model to predictive maintenance AI concept drift at a transmission substation, demonstrating all five propagation stages under non-adversarial conditions using existing SCADA telemetry and work order data. Three governance interception points are identified where active controls would have broken the propagation chain. None required new technology. The model draws on sociotechnical safety theory, human factors research, and concept drift detection, and is presented as an open analytical contribution for validation and extension.

title: Redefining the Operating Model: How AI-Native Organizations Differ from AI-Augmented Ones

detail.title: Redefining the Operating Model: How AI-Native Organizations Differ from AI-Augmented Ones
detail.abstract: Most enterprises approach artificial intelligence as an augmentation layer-bolting AI tools onto existing workflows, decision structures, and incentive systems. A smaller cohort of organizations, predominantly born-digital firms, have built their operating models around AI-first principles from inception. This paper draws a systematic distinction between AI-augmented and AI-native operating models, examining how they differ across four organizational dimensions: decision rights architecture, incentive structures, talent models, and information flows. Drawing on organizational design theory and dynamic capabilities research, the paper introduces the Algorithmic Decision Rights (ADR) framework, which classifies organizational decisions into three categories-AI-delegated, human-AI collaborative, and human-exclusive-and argues that this allocation is the single most consequential strategic choice an organization makes in its AI journey. Using comparative case analysis of born-digital companies and legacy incumbents attempting AI transformation, the paper demonstrates that augmentation strategies tend to plateau because they preserve the very decision-making structures that AI is meant to replace. The paper finds that the transition from AI-augmented to AI-native requires not incremental improvement but a discontinuous redesign of the operating model. Implications are developed for Chief Strategy Officers designing AI operating models, Chief Operating Officers restructuring workflows, and organizational design practitioners navigating the augmentation-to-native transition.

title: DESi: A Replay-Governed Epistemic Governance System for LLM-Based Research Pipelines Empirical Results Across 38 Experimental Phases

detail.title: DESi: A Replay-Governed Epistemic Governance System for LLM-Based Research Pipelines Empirical Results Across 38 Experimental Phases
detail.abstract: We present DESi (Dynamic Epistemic Sequencer-Diagnostic), a deterministic, replay-governed epistemic governance layer designed to operate above and around large language model (LLM) inference. DESi enforces a strict separation between a protected, immutable governance core and peripheral infrastructure subject to controlled evolution. Across 38 experimental phases covering epistemic failure taxonomy, search space compression, branch-isolated peripheral mutation under byte-identical protectedcore invariance, external benchmark validation, and live LLM validation with real API calls, DESi maintains replay stability at 1.0 throughout. Key empirical results include: (1) a measured recompute reduction from 36 to 4 operations (88.9%) under a frozen longitudinal benchmark with byte-identical outputs; (2) search space node reduction of 41-60% with critical branch preservation at 1.0, consistent across four independent experimental contexts; (3) trajectory-state compression of ~96.5% on 1,525 DriftBench trajectories while preserving measured drift-governance signals (preservation ratio 1.06), with explicit loss attribution identifying the Pareto-optimal compression point; (4) hallucination visibility at 1.0 under live OpenRouter API calls to IBM Granite and DeepSeek models (hallucinations are made visible and documented, not eliminated); and (5) routing cost reduction of 53.5% per redirected task with quality preservation at 1.0 (7.3% total workload reduction across the full task set). All results are derived from synthetic or locally vendored fixtures unless explicitly noted otherwise. The paper reports negative results alongside positive ones; one component (Neo4j evolution graph) is explicitly identified as overengineered. DESi does not replace LLMs, does not claim general intelligence, and makes no breakthrough assertions.

title: Redrawing the AI Map: A Theory of Accountability Boundaries in Agentic Ecosystems
affiliations: University of Pittsburgh - Katz Graduate School of Business and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Redrawing the AI Map: A Theory of Accountability Boundaries in Agentic Ecosystems
detail.abstract: Agentic AI orchestrators reduce the interface and assembly costs of composing information systems capabilities across organizational boundaries, apparently accelerating the modular forms that digital innovation theory leads us to expect. Yet AI-enabled capabilities whose outputs require evidence, review, signoff, or assignable responsibility may retain integrated accountability boundaries even when their technical interfaces become modular. We introduce accountability assets: complementary assets whose strategic value derives from making AI-supported outputs legitimate, auditable, reviewable, and assignable to a responsible party. When verification is costly and responsibility is difficult to transfer, accountability assets limit the boundary-shifting effects of agentic orchestration, even when technical decomposability is high. We further introduce rule debt: the latent governance burden that accrues when organizational decision rules migrate from formal information systems into ungoverned agentic execution environments, producing unmanaged policy artifacts that must eventually be inventoried, versioned, tested, and reconciled. The theory integrates digital innovation, transaction cost, complementary-assets, digital platform governance, and IS control perspectives to develop seven propositions explaining how agentic reductions in interface and assembly costs, verification cost, responsibility transferability, and accountability-asset cospecialization shape three capability-level boundary strategies: component, integrated, and dualtrack. The propositions further explain how appropriability conditions accountability-asset value capture, how orchestrator intent capture enables value appropriation, and how boundary misconfiguration produces rule debt. Structured theoretical illustrations across document processing, legal services, audit, clinical decision support, and procurement discipline the boundary logic. The theory advances IS scholarship by specifying when digital modularization extends to organizational disaggregation and when it does not, by extending IS control theory to agentic settings in which decision rules execute outside governed information systems, and by identifying accountability-asset cospecialization as a structural determinant of digital platform governance asymmetries.

detail.abstract: This paper examines the application of e-commerce business models, revenue strategies, digital goods, and distribution channels within the context of the Oro Savings and Sharing Multi-Purpose Cooperative (OSSMPC) in Cagayan de Oro City. Drawing on Management Information Systems (MIS) principles, the study analyzes how the cooperative’s continued reliance on manual and fragmented processes constrains operational efficiency, service accessibility, and member engagement. Using a case-based analytical approach, the paper explores the potential of integrating a web-based portal and mobile application to facilitate online transactions, digital financial services, and electronic distribution of information products. The analysis highlights the strategic value of business-to-consumer (B2C) e-commerce models, transaction fee and subscription-based revenue strategies, and digital products such as e-statements, financial literacy resources, and online learning content. Findings suggest that digital transformation can enhance operational performance through process automation, improved data management, reduced transaction costs, and expanded service reach, particularly for geographically dispersed members. However, successful implementation requires complementary investments in cybersecurity, digital literacy, governance mechanisms, and organizational change management. To support sustainable transformation, the study proposes a phased Policy Implementation Framework encompassing system integration, data governance and security, stakeholder engagement, capacity building, performance monitoring, and continuous improvement. The framework provides a practical roadmap for cooperative institutions seeking to leverage e-commerce and MIS innovations to strengthen competitiveness, improve member satisfaction, and achieve long-term organizational sustainability in the digital economy.

detail.abstract:
This monograph advances a unified theoretical and doctrinal framework for the governance of orbital civilisation. It proceeds from a single observation: the rapid commercialisation of Low Earth Orbit (LEO) has produced a class of private infrastructure operators whose strategic significance now rivals, and in certain functional domains exceeds, that of the sovereign states under whose jurisdiction they nominally operate. The author terms this condition commercial orbital sovereignty, and argues that its emergence demands a corresponding evolution in legal and political theory.

Part I — The Political Economy of Orbital Civilisation — develops the conceptual architecture for analysing orbital systems as instruments of economic power. It introduces five original constructs: orbital political economy, commercial orbital sovereignty, infrastructure dependency capture, orbital access stratification, and corporate astropolitics. These are applied to contemporary operators including SpaceX (Starlink), Amazon (Project Kuiper), Eutelsat– OneWeb, and a small constellation of insurance underwriters at Lloyd's of London whose concentrated exposure constitutes a systemic vulnerability of its own.

Part II — Post-Territorial Governance and Civilisational Autonomy — addresses the constitutional question that orbital expansion forces upon terrestrial law: whether sovereignty models predicated on geographic territoriality can retain legitimacy and operational coherence beyond the Earth-state system. The author develops Post-Territorial Governance Theory as a structured alternative to both naive orbital libertarianism and the uncritical extension of Westphalian sovereignty into space. Concepts introduced include orbital citizenship theory, mobility sovereignty, civilisational exit theory, voluntary governance through infrastructural participation, the Orbital Social Contract with its pathological counter-form of orbital feudalism, the Right to Leave Earth, and — as the author's substantive long-run hypothesis — the Severance Principle, under which voluntary orbital residence is treated as terminating the default extra-territorial jurisdiction of Earth states.

The argument is supported by analysis of the principal multilateral instruments (Outer Space Treaty 1967, Liability Convention 1972, Registration Convention 1976, Moon Agreement 1979, ITU Radio Regulations), domestic statutes (UK Outer Space Act 1986, US Commercial Space Launch Competitiveness Act 2015, Luxembourg Space Resources Law 2017), and a representative selection of decided cases and hypothetical orbital disputes constructed to expose doctrinal gaps.

The monograph concludes that orbital civilisation will require a hybrid governance architecture combining minimal multilateral safety regulation, robust private infrastructure liability, and a recognised category of post-territorial constitutional rights for orbital populations. It positions this framework as a research programme, not a manifesto: institutionally serious, doctrinally rigorous, and operationally implementable.

detail.abstract: How do investments in innovation translate into future productivity growth? Empirically answering this question is challenging. R&D spending is an observed input into the innovation process, but mapping it to productivity growth requires assumptions about the depreciation of R&D capital, gestation lags, and how well such expenditures capture true innovative effort (Hall, 2007). Patents, an alternative measure, capture successful innovations but vary widely in novelty (Kelly et al., 2021) and economic value (Kogan et al., 2017). Firms may forgo patenting to preserve secrecy, while others patent strategically to protect existing products even when their underlying innovations are marginal.
